payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host a TypeScript AI assistant that saves conversations in Postgres? > [What belongs on the server and in Postgres?](https://www.prisma.io#what-belongs-on-the-server-and-in-postgres)
payload.content:
## [What belongs on the server and in Postgres?](https://www.prisma.io#what-belongs-on-the-server-and-in-postgres)

For chat between users, use the [realtime chat database guide](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/realtime-chat-database) to compare durable messages, room permissions, presence and delivery after a reconnect.

The server authenticates the user, checks conversation access, calls the model provider and writes messages. Keep the model API key and database credentials in server-side configuration. The browser should call an application endpoint rather than connect with a database password.

Store conversations with an owner or account identifier. Store messages with a conversation reference, role, content and processing state. A request identifier helps the server recognize a retried send instead of creating another copy of the user's message.

Keep persistence separate from the model's context window. You can retain a conversation in Postgres while sending only selected messages or a summary to the model. Decide retention and deletion behavior for customer conversations before the app starts collecting sensitive text.

To add a rating to a saved answer, use the [assistant feedback storage guide](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/ai-assistant-feedback). It covers one vote per user and message, ownership checks and repeat submissions.

## [Which hosting setup fits the assistant?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-setup-fits-the-assistant)

These options are ordered alphabetically by app host.

| App host | When to choose it | Database and response work | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify + Prisma Postgres | Your framework already uses [Netlify's deployment workflow](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/create-deploys/). | Deploy the server features too, set the database URL in server configuration and check the runtime limits for your model calls. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | You want the TypeScript server and database declared in one project. | Configure the Composer module, database dependency and model API secret. Check [request and streaming behavior](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout). | 
| Vercel + Prisma Postgres | Your app already follows Vercel's framework workflow. | Its [streaming function documentation](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/streaming-functions) explains response delivery; the app must still save conversation data. | 

Place the database-calling server [near Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/nodejs-database-regions). Changing app hosts is optional: Prisma Postgres accepts ordinary PostgreSQL connections from a supported server runtime.

payload.content:
## [3. Read history through an authorized endpoint](https://www.prisma.io#3-read-history-through-an-authorized-endpoint)

The demonstration account is `42`. This query joins the conversation's ownership to its messages:

The inner query selects the latest 50 messages; the outer query puts that page in display order. For the two demonstration messages, it returns the user question followed by the assistant reply, with their IDs. In the server, bind query values as parameters and derive the authorized account from the verified session. Apply that check to writes and deletes too. If you use row-level security, configure the relevant roles and policies as well.

Use the smallest returned message ID as the cursor when requesting an older page. The demonstration page starts at ID `1`, so this next-page query correctly returns no older rows:

The application should bind the conversation, verified account and cursor as parameters. A new conversation loads the first query without a cursor; subsequent requests use the smallest ID from the previous page. If parallel generations need a strict conversational turn sequence, model that sequence explicitly; an insertion ID alone does not define the order in which concurrent work completes.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host a TypeScript AI assistant that saves conversations in Postgres? > [4. Define generation and interruption states](https://www.prisma.io#4-define-generation-and-interruption-states)
payload.content:
## [4. Define generation and interruption states](https://www.prisma.io#4-define-generation-and-interruption-states)

Save the user message before calling the model. Create an assistant message in `pending` state, then save its content and mark it `completed` when generation succeeds. Use distinct request keys for the user message and assistant reply, with duplicate-request handling in the server.

Decide how interrupted work becomes `failed` or resumes. Persist a start time or job identifier if you need a recovery process to find abandoned pending messages after a crash. Catching errors in a handler alone cannot update a row after the process has stopped.

For token-level resumption, persist chunks or events before relying on them as durable history. The [Open Chat walkthrough](https://www.prisma.io/blog/building-open-chat) describes an event-log design with Prisma Streams. Saving only the final response has a smaller implementation, but loses unsaved output if generation is interrupted.

payload.content:
## [5. Deploy and test a return visit](https://www.prisma.io#5-deploy-and-test-a-return-visit)

For a project with a `build` script and the `module.ts` prepared in step 1, authenticate, build the app and deploy a separate review stage. Configure the project region through the [deployment setup](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/deploy) if it is not already set. These commands use the current [Prisma 8 release candidate CLI](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/release-status) explicitly, so an older project-local CLI is not selected:

Open the service URL returned by the deployment. Confirm that its database target is the intended review resource before applying migrations or testing writes. An externally supplied URL must point to a separate test database; changing the stage name does not isolate an external database by itself.

Prisma Compute runs deployed services on Bun, so check runtime-dependent packages. Its [request timeout](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout) gives a service 60 seconds to start responding; a response that has started streaming is not subject to that first-byte deadline.

Test a saved conversation after refreshing, signing out and signing back in. Verify that another account cannot read its messages. Interrupt a generation and check that the UI and database state match the recovery behavior you chose. Also rehearse deleting a conversation and its associated messages.

## [When should I choose a different setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-a-different-setup)

Prisma Compute currently does not host WebSocket servers. Use an HTTP streaming design it supports, or choose another app host if WebSocket server support is a requirement. Streaming an HTTP response also does not guarantee that an in-process generation job survives a restart or deployment.

Choose database hosting with the regions, extensions and recovery features your customer data requires. Prisma Postgres has [plan-dependent snapshots](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) and no point-in-time recovery yet (it is coming in November 2026). Keep long-term history, backups and model-provider costs as separate decisions when estimating the app's operating budget.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting?
payload.content:
## TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting?

`streamText` or your provider's streaming API. Then check the host's limit for a streamed response. Vercel counts the whole stream against `maxDuration` (with fluid compute, the default for projects created since April 23, 2025: 300 seconds by default, up to 800 on Pro and Enterprise), Google Cloud Run's request timeout defaults to 5 minutes and goes up to 60, Netlify stops synchronous and streaming functions at 60 seconds, Railway allows 15 minutes while data keeps flowing, and Cloudflare Workers have no wall-clock limit while the client stays connected. Turn off proxy buffering, and move agent runs that take longer than your host allows into a background job. On [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute), a service has 60 seconds to send its first bytes, and a response that has started streaming is not cut off when it passes 60 seconds.

A chat request that waits for the full model answer fails in one of two ways. Either nothing appears until the whole answer has been generated, or the request ends with a timeout before any of it arrives. Long answers, reasoning models and tool calls make both worse, because the time until the last token grows while the user sees nothing. The fix is to stream the answer as the model produces it and to give the whole stream enough time on your host.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The fix below works on any host. The host and library limits on this page link to their documentation, checked on October 22, 2026.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [Which timeout are you hitting?](https://www.prisma.io#which-timeout-are-you-hitting)
payload.content:
## [Which timeout are you hitting?](https://www.prisma.io#which-timeout-are-you-hitting)

What the user sees, and when, points to the cause.

| What you see | Likely cause | Check | 
|---|---|---|
| Nothing for a while, then the whole answer at once | The handler waits for the full answer, or a proxy buffers the stream | Whether the route returns before the model finishes, and the proxy's buffering setting | 
| A `504` with `FUNCTION_INVOCATION_TIMEOUT` on Vercel | The invocation ran past its maximum duration, which includes streaming | `maxDuration` for the route and your plan's maximum | 
| The function stops after 10 to 60 seconds on Vercel | The project runs without fluid compute, so the limits in Vercel's current tables don't apply to it | Whether fluid compute is on in the project's Functions settings, then `maxDuration` | 
| The answer stops partway at the same time on every long reply | A limit on the total request time | The host's limit for a streamed response, in the table below | 
| A `504 Gateway Time-out` from `openresty` after about 60 seconds on Prisma Compute | No bytes were sent within 60 seconds | Whether the route sends something before the model's first token | 
| A Cloudflare `524` page | Cloudflare's proxy got no response from your server within its read timeout | Whether the response starts within 125 seconds | 
| The stream dies during a long tool call | An idle timeout between two chunks | Proxy read timeouts, such as nginx's 60-second default |

payload.content:
| The stream dies during a long tool call | An idle timeout between two chunks | Proxy read timeouts, such as nginx's 60-second default | 

To tell a buffering proxy from a route that doesn't stream, call the route with [`curl -N`](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#-N), which turns off curl's own output buffering. If curl prints the answer in pieces and the browser shows it all at once, look at the proxy or the client code. A buffering proxy holds the response for curl too, so if curl waits, send the same request once through the proxy and once straight to the app, for example to its port on the server. If curl also waits on the direct request, the route itself isn't streaming.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [Why it happens](https://www.prisma.io#why-it-happens)
payload.content:
## [Why it happens](https://www.prisma.io#why-it-happens)

Chat code often starts with a call that resolves when the model has finished, such as the AI SDK's `generateText` or a provider call without streaming. The server can't send anything until that call returns, so the user's wait is the model's total generation time, and the host's request limit applies to all of it.

Streaming changes what the user waits for: the server returns a response at once and writes each token as the model produces it. It doesn't remove the host's limits. On [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration), the maximum duration "includes time spent processing the request and sending the response, including streamed responses." So a streamed answer that runs longer than the limit is still cut off.

A proxy in front of the server can undo streaming. [nginx](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html#proxy_buffering) buffers responses from the proxied server by default (`proxy_buffering on`), so the browser gets chunks in batches or at the end.

payload.content:
## [1. Stream the model's answer from the route](https://www.prisma.io#1-stream-the-models-answer-from-the-route)

With the AI SDK, `streamText` starts the model call, and `createUIMessageStreamResponse` with `toUIMessageStream` returns a streaming response that the `useChat` hook reads, as in the [Next.js quickstart](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/getting-started/nextjs-app-router). Older examples write the same response as `result.toUIMessageStreamResponse()`, which the [`streamText` reference](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/reference/ai-sdk-core/stream-text) still lists. This route was type-checked and run with `ai` 7.0.148 and `@ai-sdk/openai` 4.0.99:

Passing `req.signal` stops the model call, and the tokens it uses, when the user closes the tab. It also stops it when a proxy drops the connection or the user refreshes, and then the answer is lost. If you save answers, leave out `abortSignal` and call `result.consumeStream()` without awaiting it: generation then runs to the end after a disconnect, and the `onEnd` callback of `toUIMessageStream` can save the finished messages, as the AI SDK's [message persistence docs](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-ui/chatbot-message-persistence#handling-client-disconnects) show.

On the client, `useChat` from `@ai-sdk/react` posts to `/api/chat` and renders each message's `parts` as they arrive, as the [AI SDK quickstart](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/getting-started/nextjs-app-router) shows. Tutorials written for AI SDK 4 use `toDataStreamResponse()` and `handleSubmit`, which AI SDK 5 replaced ([migration guide](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/migration-guides/migration-guide-5-0)), so check the docs for the version in your `package.json` before copying code.

payload.content:
## [2. Or stream server-sent events without the AI SDK](https://www.prisma.io#2-or-stream-server-sent-events-without-the-ai-sdk)

A provider SDK can stream on its own. With the [OpenAI SDK](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/streaming-responses), `stream: true` returns an iterable of events, and the text arrives in `response.output_text.delta` events. This route forwards them as [server-sent events](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events), type-checked and run with `openai` 7.42.0:

The first comment line goes out before the model call starts, and the heartbeat sends another every 15 seconds while a long tool call or reasoning step produces no text. MDN describes comment lines as a way "to prevent connections from timing out." On the client, read `response.body` with a reader and append each `data:` line's text as it arrives.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [3. Give the stream enough time on your host](https://www.prisma.io#3-give-the-stream-enough-time-on-your-host)
payload.content:
## [3. Give the stream enough time on your host](https://www.prisma.io#3-give-the-stream-enough-time-on-your-host)

Compare your longest answer, including tool calls, with the limit for a streamed response on your host. These hosts are ordered alphabetically:

| Host | Before the first byte | A response that is streaming | 
|---|---|---|
| Cloudflare Workers | No separate limit | [No wall-clock limit](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#duration) while the client stays connected. CPU time is limited separately: 10 ms on Free, 30 seconds by default and up to 5 minutes on Paid; waiting on `fetch()` doesn't count. | 
| Google Cloud Run | Part of the request timeout | The [request timeout](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/request-timeout) is 5 minutes by default and can be raised to 60 minutes; long-running requests, [WebSocket streams](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/triggering/websockets) included, are subject to it. For more than 15 minutes, Google recommends retries and clients that can reconnect. | 
| Netlify Functions | Part of the function's limit | 60 seconds for [synchronous](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/configuration/) (not configurable) and [streaming](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/api/) functions. Background functions run for 15 minutes but answer the client with a `202` at once. | 
| Prisma Compute | [60 seconds](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout) | Not cut off when it passes 60 seconds. The docs advise keeping data flowing and having the client reconnect for anything long-lived. | 
| Railway | 5 minutes with no data | [15 minutes](https://docs.railway.com/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits) if data keeps transferring; closed after 5 minutes with no data. |

With [fluid compute](https://vercel.com/docs/fluid-compute) (the default for projects created since April 23, 2025): 300 seconds on Hobby; 300 seconds by default and up to 800 on Pro and Enterprise (1,800 in beta). The Edge runtime must start responding within 25 seconds and can stream for up to 300. |

payload.content:
## [4. Turn off buffering in proxies](https://www.prisma.io#4-turn-off-buffering-in-proxies)

If nginx sits in front of the app, turn off buffering for the chat route, or send `X-Accel-Buffering: no` from the route as the second example does. nginx's [`proxy_read_timeout`](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html#proxy_read_timeout) defaults to 60 seconds between two reads, so keep the heartbeat shorter than that or raise the timeout. The AI SDK route in step 1 sends no heartbeat: after its first event, nothing goes out until the model produces output, so raise `proxy_read_timeout` for it when a tool call or reasoning step can run longer than 60 seconds:

Behind Cloudflare's proxy, the server has to start responding within 125 seconds or the visitor gets a [`524` error](https://developers.cloudflare.com/support/troubleshooting/http-status-codes/cloudflare-5xx-errors/error-524/). Enterprise plans can raise that to 6,000 seconds. A route that returns its streaming response at once, with an early comment line, starts responding well inside that window.

payload.section: [5. Move long agent runs out of the request](https://www.prisma.io#5-move-long-agent-runs-out-of-the-request)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [5. Move long agent runs out of the request](https://www.prisma.io#5-move-long-agent-runs-out-of-the-request)
payload.content:
## [5. Move long agent runs out of the request](https://www.prisma.io#5-move-long-agent-runs-out-of-the-request)

An agent loop that can run longer than your host allows doesn't belong in one HTTP request. Save the job, start it in a worker or a background job, and have the browser follow its progress: poll an endpoint, reconnect to a stream that reads saved output, or use the AI SDK's [resumable streams](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-ui/chatbot-resume-streams). If you use resumable streams, don't pass the request's abort signal to the model call, because a disconnect would then cancel the generation the client wants to reconnect to. Add a separate stop endpoint for user cancellation, as the [AI SDK docs](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/troubleshooting/abort-breaks-resumable-streams) describe. Save the user's message before you call the model, so a dropped connection doesn't lose the question as well as the answer.

payload.section: [How to choose hosting for a streaming chat app](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-choose-hosting-for-a-streaming-chat-app)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [How to choose hosting for a streaming chat app](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-choose-hosting-for-a-streaming-chat-app)
payload.content:
## [How to choose hosting for a streaming chat app](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-choose-hosting-for-a-streaming-chat-app)

Pick the host by the longest answer you need to deliver and by the connections your app holds open:

- **Answers finish in a few minutes, and the app already runs on Vercel:** stream, and set `maxDuration` to cover the longest answer.
- **Answers or agent runs can take longer than a serverless limit:** a host with a longer request limit, such as Google Cloud Run (up to 60 minutes per request) or Railway (15 minutes per request while data flows), a long-running server on Render, Fly.io or a VM you run, or a background job that the browser follows.
- **The app needs WebSocket connections:** a host that runs a WebSocket server, such as [Railway](https://docs.railway.com/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits), where WebSocket connections are exempt from the duration limits, [Render](https://render.com/docs/websocket), which doesn't enforce a maximum duration for them, or [Fly.io](https://fly.io/docs/networking/websockets/), whose proxy doesn't close idle WebSocket connections. On [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/websockets), a WebSocket connection closes when the function reaches its maximum duration.
- **Answers start streaming within 60 seconds but can run longer, and you want the server and its Postgres database in one project:** Prisma Compute with Prisma Postgres, covered next (no WebSocket servers today; support is planned for early 2027).

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)
payload.content:
## [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)

Prisma Compute fits a TypeScript chat endpoint that starts streaming within 60 seconds: its [request timeout](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout) applies only to the wait for the first bytes, so a streamed answer that runs longer is not cut off when it passes 60 seconds. [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) hosts TypeScript apps built for Node.js, Bun or Next.js, and deployed apps run on Bun. It doesn't require Prisma ORM or Prisma Postgres.

A Next.js app deploys with [Prisma Composer](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer)'s `nextjs` build adapter and `output: "standalone"`, as the [Next.js guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/frameworks/nextjs) shows, so the chat route stays a route handler. Keep the model's API key in the deployment's secret configuration, as the [secrets guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-app-secrets) describes. The 60 seconds are counted by Compute's ingress, so `maxDuration` and timeouts inside the route don't change them.

When the 60 seconds pass with nothing sent, the client gets a `504` and Compute cancels the request. Your code sees that as an aborted `req.signal`, not as an error in the logs. While a stream waits on the model, the instance uses little CPU but stays running, and the [pricing docs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/pricing) bill provisioned memory for that time and active CPU only while code runs. The Free plan includes 1M requests, 360 GB-hours of memory and 4 active vCPU-hours per month, with no credit card.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > TypeScript AI chat app times out before the answer appears: how do I stream the response and choose hosting? > [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)
payload.content:
Conversations can live in [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres) in the same project. The [conversation history guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/ai-assistant-conversation-history) covers the schema and ownership checks, and the [AI SDK guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/integrations/ai-sdk) saves each chat from the stream's `onEnd` callback with Prisma ORM. Any Postgres client works.

Know the limits before you rely on it:

- Compute does not run WebSocket servers today; support is planned for early 2027. Stream over HTTP or server-sent events, or run the socket server on another host.
- The docs don't state a maximum length for a started stream. They say to keep data flowing rather than let it sit idle, and to have the client reconnect for anything long-lived ([streaming responses](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout#streaming-responses)), so send a heartbeat during long tool calls and use a background job the client reconnects to for agent runs.
- The 60 seconds include everything before the first byte. A route that awaits a slow tool call or a long reasoning step before sending anything gets a `504`, so send an early event first.
- Work after the response, with `waitUntil` or `KeepAwakeGuard`, is best effort. It keeps the instance awake, but it doesn't retry failures or continue through a restart or a new deployment ([Keeping instances awake](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/keeping-instances-awake)). Generation that continues after the browser disconnects, as with `consumeStream()`, is background work in this sense. An agent run that must finish needs saved progress and a separate trigger.

payload.content:
- Each service runs in one region, and Compute has no edge runtime ([Known limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations)). Pick the region nearest your users or your database.
- If your answers fit inside a serverless limit and the app already runs on Vercel or Netlify, moving hosts doesn't fix a timeout. Stream and set the limit where the app runs.

payload.content:
## [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)

Stream from the first version of the chat route, even when answers are short, so a slower model delays the first token instead of the whole answer. Set an explicit limit on the model call below the host's limit, with the AI SDK's [`timeout` option](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/reference/ai-sdk-core/stream-text) or an [`AbortSignal.timeout()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal/timeout_static), so your code returns an error the client can show instead of a gateway page. On Prisma Compute, keep a timeout on work before the first byte under 60 seconds, for example 50, as the [request timeout docs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout#what-your-service-sees) advise. Log how long the first token and the full answer take, and compare the slowest answers with your host's limit before you add tools or switch to a slower model.

payload.content:
## [When this fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#when-this-fix-doesnt-apply)

If the error comes from the model provider, such as a `429` rate limit or a provider timeout, streaming and hosting changes won't help; check the provider's error and retry rules. If the browser gives up first, look for a client-side timeout in a `fetch` wrapper or HTTP client. And if the request fails in under a second, the route is erroring, not timing out: read the server logs before changing limits.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host an AI API that charges credits?
payload.content:
## How should I host an AI API that charges credits?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)fits a small team that wants its API, saved usage and deployment configuration in one project. Vercel or Netlify with Prisma Postgres can also fit an existing app. The host runs the API; your application must define reservations, retries, settlement and customer-visible balances.

A customer with ten credits can send two requests at the same time. If both handlers read ten and each decides to spend seven, a check in application memory can approve work the balance cannot cover. Choose the hosting workflow you like, then enforce admission in the database.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. Provider and PostgreSQL sources linked here were checked on October 22, 2026.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host an AI API that charges credits? > [What must the setup keep reliable?](https://www.prisma.io#what-must-the-setup-keep-reliable)
payload.content:
## [What must the setup keep reliable?](https://www.prisma.io#what-must-the-setup-keep-reliable)

Keep an account balance, a history of credit changes and a record for each logical AI request. The history explains the balance; the request record explains whether work is reserved, running, completed or awaiting reconciliation. Keep model usage and the pricing rule used for the charge with that record.

Derive the account from verified authentication and calculate the charge on the server. A browser or model response must not choose the account balance or its own price. An AI assistant can write the implementation, but tests must prove its behavior with concurrent requests, retries and failures.

Separate the prices you charge customers from the [infrastructure meters](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-hosting-cost-visibility). A model request can cause several database queries and an app response. Those costs need their own budget even when the customer's credit price is fixed.

These options are alphabetical by app host and can use Prisma Postgres.

## [1. Create a separate development ledger](https://www.prisma.io#1-create-a-separate-development-ledger)

Create a development Prisma Postgres database in [Console](https://console.prisma.io). Use fictional accounts and credits, separate from live customers. Prisma ORM is optional.

Apply schema migrations through the database's [direct connection](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database). Use its pooled URL for ordinary TCP application connections; the [Prisma Postgres serverless driver](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/serverless-driver) requires the direct URL. Define constraints for nonnegative balances, valid request states and unique account/request identifiers.

payload.content:
## [2. Prove the conditional balance change](https://www.prisma.io#2-prove-the-conditional-balance-change)

With `psql` installed, open a direct connection to the development database. Paste this SQL into one session:

The first update returns `remaining = 3`; another seven-credit debit then returns no rows. PostgreSQL rechecks an update's condition after a competing writer commits under its [default isolation level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html).

This demonstrates one admission rule, not a complete credit ledger. The second update is another debit attempt, not a deduplicated retry. Production code needs saved request identifiers, transaction boundaries and a policy for database errors. The temporary table disappears when the session ends.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host an AI API that charges credits? > [3. Reserve, call the model and settle](https://www.prisma.io#3-reserve-call-the-model-and-settle)
payload.content:
## [3. Reserve, call the model and settle](https://www.prisma.io#3-reserve-call-the-model-and-settle)

For an implemented ledger, make the sequence explicit:

1. Authenticate the account and assign or reuse the logical request ID.
2. Start a transaction, lock the account's wallet row, and look up the request by account and request ID. If it exists, compare the validated inputs and any client-requested credit limit with its saved inputs or fingerprint; reject a mismatch. For a matching retry, end the transaction and return the saved state under its original pricing rules. For a new request, check the balance and persist the validated inputs and model/work limits, or an immutable durable reference to them. Save a canonical fingerprint and the server-decided credit amount and pricing version, reserve the credits, mark the request reserved and add its credit-history entry in that same transaction, then commit. Roll back a rejected request.
3. Atomically claim the reserved request by changing its state to running, and commit that change before submitting it to the model. Only the process that won this transition may submit the call. Make the call outside the transaction with a deadline, and save the provider request identifier when it becomes available.
4. In a new transaction, conditionally change the request from an allowed unfinished state to its final state. Only the transaction that wins this transition may apply the settlement or release to the wallet and add the corresponding credit-history entry; commit those changes together. A retry that finds a final request returns its saved result, while other invalid transitions are rejected.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host an AI API that charges credits? > [3. Reserve, call the model and settle](https://www.prisma.io#3-reserve-call-the-model-and-settle)
payload.content:
When a model call times out, its outcome may be uncertain. Keep that request in a state your reconciliation process can inspect rather than immediately refunding and sending the same expensive work again. A database transaction cannot make an external API call happen exactly once.

Deploy a recovery worker that periodically finds reservations whose processing deadline has passed. A still-reserved request can be claimed through the same atomic transition. An expired running request is uncertain until the provider confirms its outcome, even when no provider identifier was saved: the process may have stopped after submission. Do not automatically release its credits or resubmit it. Check the provider's result or usage records when available; otherwise hold the reservation for an explicit review policy. The [Postgres worker guide](https://www.prisma.io/blog/you-dont-need-a-job-queue-postgres-already-has-skip-locked#where-to-run-the-worker) explains the always-on host needed for a polling process. Saving a reservation alone does not schedule its recovery.

For variable-cost work, reserve an explicit upper bound and enforce the corresponding model-output or work limit. Define what happens when a request reaches it. Fixed-price credits need a different settlement rule from pass-through token pricing.

payload.content:
## [4. Deploy and test the whole request lifecycle](https://www.prisma.io#4-deploy-and-test-the-whole-request-lifecycle)

Follow [Compute getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started), or [port the existing API](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/porting-an-app), to configure the server and its inputs. Keep model keys in server-side secret configuration.

A database created by a Composer module is separate from a Console-created development database. Prepare every review and production target through the [migration workflow](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/production-database-migrations) before serving customer work. A configured `postgres()` data contract can apply migrations during deployment; `rawPostgres()` and manually supplied URLs require your own migration step.

Test simultaneous requests, repeated IDs, insufficient credits, a model failure, a timeout after success and a process restart between reservation and settlement. An API response and the customer's usage screen should agree with the saved request state.

payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Choose a billing service if you need an existing product to own subscriptions, credit expiry or invoicing rules. If Stripe funds the wallet, verify payment events and deduplicate top-ups; the [Stripe hosting guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/nextjs-stripe-subscriptions) covers that boundary.

Compute has [60 seconds to start a response](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout). Long-running requests need a suitable durable worker design, not an in-memory promise treated as a queue. Check the runtime and recovery requirements before selecting the worker host. Prisma Postgres has [automatic snapshots on paid plans, created daily on days with database activity](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups), with no point-in-time recovery yet (it is coming in November 2026); choose another database if you need that recovery window today.

## How can I check my app and database in one place?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)gives a TypeScript team one project to inspect through Console and the CLI, with Query Insights for database behavior. Use an external check of a real application route as well: an available service and a reachable database do not prove that sign-in or saving a record works.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)8 min read

A dashboard can show a running server while customers see an error. The server may have the wrong database credentials, an unapplied schema change or a broken login callback. A useful hosting setup helps you tell those failures apart.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. Provider documentation linked here was checked on October 22, 2026. Prisma ORM is optional.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How can I check my app and database in one place? > [Which checks answer which question?](https://www.prisma.io#which-checks-answer-which-question)
payload.content:
## [Which checks answer which question?](https://www.prisma.io#which-checks-answer-which-question)

Keep process availability, dependency readiness and customer success separate. That distinction makes an alert actionable.

| Check | What it tells you | What it leaves untested | 
|---|---|---|
| A small HTTP response without a database query | The service can answer a request. | Database access, authentication and saved records. | 
| A bounded database query through the app's configured client | The deployed app can reach and query its database. | Whether the correct business operation and permissions work. | 
| A representative user workflow with a dedicated test account | The tested sign-in, read or write path works through the public app. | Other users, untested paths and future requests. | 

For example, an order portal might have an inexpensive liveness route, a restricted readiness route that checks its required table, and a monitored test account that reads a fictional order. Use a write test only when its records and cleanup are clearly separated from customer work.

payload.content:
## [Which platforms make investigation manageable?](https://www.prisma.io#which-platforms-make-investigation-manageable)

Choose among these alphabetically listed options around the application you run and the evidence you need during an incident.

| Setup | Useful visibility | Work you still configure | 
|---|---|---|
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | Services and databases in one project, [version-targeted service logs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service) and [Query Insights](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/query-insights). | Application checks, alerts and an external test of the public URL. | 
| Railway services and Postgres | A [project canvas](https://docs.railway.com/projects) for related services and [CPU, memory, disk and network metrics](https://docs.railway.com/observability/metrics). | Application latency/error telemetry, database operations and customer workflow checks. | 
| Vercel + managed Postgres | [Request-grouped runtime logs](https://vercel.com/docs/logs/runtime) fit teams already investigating a Next.js app on Vercel. | Database-provider diagnostics and a way to correlate them with app requests. | 

Prisma Compute is a practical default for a small TypeScript team that wants to find and manage the service and database in the same project. Console groups those resources, while the external monitor supplies alerts. This is a shared project for investigation, rather than a single screen that certifies every customer workflow. If you already have a monitoring system that works across several providers, keep it.

## [1. Record the actual production targets](https://www.prisma.io#1-record-the-actual-production-targets)

Start with an already deployed application; [getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started) covers the first deployment. Open its project in Console and record the branch serving customers, the live service version and the database. A [platform branch](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/branching) groups deployed service versions. The production branch is the first branch in the project, usually `main`; a named Composer stage deploy creates a separate platform branch for its services and databases. Copy the actual branch name from Console when inspecting that stage. Verify the branch in Console rather than assuming your local Git checkout selects production. Record the public URL and deployment commit too.

For an existing service, these [CLI commands](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service) inspect its version and recent logs. Replace `orders`, `web` and `main` with the actual project, service and confirmed production branch:

The output belongs to your deployment, so its version identifiers and log lines will differ. These are inspection commands, not a fix. Build logs are available in Console; service logs can return `FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE` when the platform cannot serve logs for the selected version.

payload.content:
## [2. Probe the same connection the app uses](https://www.prisma.io#2-probe-the-same-connection-the-app-uses)

Use the same database client and credentials as the app. In Composer, the app's TypeScript deployment configuration lists the database under `deps`; the server reads its connection details with `service.load()`. The [Bun connection guide](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/bun-sql-hosting) shows the server-side code. An externally supplied URL instead uses the configuration steps in [Service input](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/service-input). A probe using a separate administrator connection can pass while the app's own connection is broken.

Keep the query small and impose a timeout on connection acquisition and execution. Test a required application table with a read that returns no customer payload. Avoid a full-table count, schema migration or repeated write as a routine readiness check. Return a bounded failure response rather than making a health request wait indefinitely.

Keep a simple liveness check independent of Postgres. If the database becomes unavailable, restarting every healthy app instance can add load without correcting the dependency failure.

For a Bun server, save the following helper in `health.ts`. It checks connectivity through the existing Bun SQL client:

A reachable development database produces HTTP `200` and `ready`; an unavailable database or a probe exceeding this example's two-second budget produces HTTP `503` and `unavailable`. Cancelling the query might not stop it immediately. Use a read-only query so a late-running check cannot change data. This query checks connectivity; replace it with a small application-table read when you need to test schema readiness. For example, `SELECT 1 FROM app_settings LIMIT 1` verifies that a table can be queried without returning its contents; replace the example table name with a required table in your schema and adjust the success test to accept an empty result. Keep the existing liveness route free of database work.

payload.content:
Integrate this with the existing server rather than replacing its application routes. The following wrapper accepts the existing request handler, SQL client and monitor token, and forwards only the two health paths to the adapter:

Save the adapter as `health-handler.ts` and the wrapper as `with-health-routes.ts`. Set the existing `Bun.serve` call's `fetch` option to `withHealthRoutes(appHandler, sql, monitorToken)`, importing the wrapper into that server file. Here `appHandler` is the app's current handler and `sql` is its current client. On Compute, follow [Service input](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/service-input) to declare a monitor-token configuration field in `service.ts`, name its secret platform variable with `envSecret(...)` in `module.ts`, and read its value on the server. payload.content:
## [3. Correlate an outside-in check with the diagnostics](https://www.prisma.io#3-correlate-an-outside-in-check-with-the-diagnostics)

Run a check from outside the hosting platform against the intended public URL. Confirm that it reaches the application rather than a cached static response or a login redirect that always returns success. A dedicated test account can exercise authentication and one representative saved-data read.

For example, Better Stack documents [creating an API monitor with an authentication header](https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/api-monitor/) and [choosing notification channels](https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/monitoring-start/). Set the deployed readiness URL, supply the dedicated monitor credential through its request headers, choose the expected success status and timeout, and select an actual responder. Test the failure notification before relying on it. This HTTP check covers the readiness route; a customer journey needs an additional authenticated workflow test.

Configure the monitor to send an `X-Monitor-Id` header identifying that monitor, and record that header with the request timestamp in the server's access logs so you can match failed probes to activity. Record the live deployment version from `service show` alongside the monitor result. In [Prisma Console](https://console.prisma.io), open the affected project's database and its [Query Insights](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/query-insights) view. Compare query latency and repeated SQL in the failure's time window with service logs. Slow SQL calls for query investigation; a request that never reaches SQL calls for a different investigation.

payload.content:
## [4. Test the alert and its operating cost](https://www.prisma.io#4-test-the-alert-and-its-operating-cost)

In an [isolated review environment](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/typescript-test-environment), temporarily pass the health adapter a separate Bun SQL client with a deliberately invalid test connection URL. This tests failure handling without changing the database connection supplied by Composer. Verify that the dependency check fails, the liveness route still explains whether the server responds, and an alert reaches the channel your team actually watches. Restore the test configuration afterward.

Before applying the configuration to production, review the interval, timeout, access control and [usage cost](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-hosting-cost-visibility). Prisma Compute meters requests and active resources, and Prisma Postgres meters operations. A probe should earn the work it causes, especially for an app used only occasionally.

## [When is a different setup a better fit?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-a-different-setup-a-better-fit)

Use an existing cross-provider observability system when you need unified tracing across many services or organizations. Console and CLI inspection are not a substitute for that requirement, and a platform status page cannot certify your application's business rules.

Check [Compute's current limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations) for log availability and runtime requirements. Do not choose a host on the assumption that retaining an open connection, an in-memory monitor or a local file will survive a redeploy. Keep the check's state and alerting outside the process it is checking.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)7 min read

An exported customer portal might contain a frontend, server routes and calls to a managed backend. Getting its repository onto another host is one task. Moving the customer accounts, documents and data that those calls depend on is another.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The official sources linked here were checked on October 29, 2026. payload.content:
## [What did the builder actually export?](https://www.prisma.io#what-did-the-builder-actually-export)

Inspect the repository before choosing a deployment preset. Read its package scripts, framework configuration, server entry points, environment-variable names and backend SDK imports. Have your assistant list the services each feature calls, rather than describe the project only as a React app.

[Lovable's external-hosting guide](https://docs.lovable.dev/tips-tricks/external-deployment-hosting) distinguishes newer TanStack Start apps from older React and Vite apps. The former include a server part; the latter can build to static frontend files. A static-file deployment cannot execute server functions simply because the landing page loads.

[Bolt's Git integration](https://support.bolt.new/integrations/git) provides a source-control path, and its [project-management guide](https://support.bolt.new/managing-projects/projects-files) covers downloading a project. Check the exported application rather than assuming that every Bolt project has the same framework or database arrangement.

Make a short inventory for your app:

| Part | Evidence to inspect | Deployment consequence | 
|---|---|---|
| Browser frontend | Its build output, routing and public configuration. | Static output needs hosting and route handling; server-rendered output also needs a server runtime. | 
| Server code | API routes, server functions, webhooks and private keys. | Deploy these to a compatible runtime and recreate their server-side secrets. | 
| Backend services | Database SDK calls, auth redirects, file buckets, functions and realtime subscriptions. | Preserve those services or implement and test their replacements. |

## [Which hosting setup should I choose?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-setup-should-i-choose)

The hosts below are ordered alphabetically. Keep the existing backend during an initial frontend move when that avoids changing two systems at once.

| App host | Useful fit | What you manage | 
|---|---|---|
| [Netlify](https://docs.netlify.com/build/frameworks/overview/) | A frontend or full-stack framework supported by its deployment adapter. | Build settings, the framework's server support, environment variables, route behavior and the connection to the existing backend or a separate API. | 
| Prisma Compute | You want a TypeScript application server and its Postgres dependency declared together, with CLI-driven deployment and inspection. | The Composer declaration, a build compatible with Bun, application authorization, migrations and any backend services you replace. No WebSocket servers or persistent writable filesystem. See [limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations). | 
| [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/frameworks) | An exported app whose framework matches its supported build and server deployment path. | Framework configuration, server execution limits, environment variables, authentication callbacks and the database or backend connection. | 

Prisma's integration is useful once your team owns the server's business logic: the service and database dependency live in the same declaration, so an assistant can inspect their relationship while deploying or debugging. [Composer's plain Postgres path](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases) supports the database client you already use; Prisma ORM is optional.

payload.content:
## [1. Establish a working export](https://www.prisma.io#1-establish-a-working-export)

Export or sync the repository, keep its lockfile, and run its documented production build in a clean local checkout as a validation step. Inspect the output and start procedure. For server-rendered apps, follow the framework's deployment adapter rather than treating the build output as a directory of static pages.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host my exported Bolt or Lovable app? > [2. Recreate configuration deliberately](https://www.prisma.io#2-recreate-configuration-deliberately)
payload.content:
## [2. Recreate configuration deliberately](https://www.prisma.io#2-recreate-configuration-deliberately)

Set the public backend configuration before the new host runs its deployment build. For example, a Vite app embeds values such as `VITE_SUPABASE_URL` in the browser bundle at build time; changing those values requires rebuilding and redeploying. Recreate private secrets in the new server environment. Builder-managed secrets are not something to recover from Git. Keep database passwords, payment secrets and privileged backend keys out of browser bundles and public build variables.

A Supabase publishable key is designed for browser use with the appropriate authorization policies; it is different from a database password or privileged service key. Check the app's policies and server checks instead of treating every variable with a public prefix as an administrative credential.

Update authentication redirect URLs for the preview and eventual production domains. Build and deploy the configured preview, then test a nested route by opening it directly, a server-rendered page if present, and a real server operation. Verify sign-in, sign-out, password reset, document access and an unauthorized access attempt. These checks catch broken routes and backend connections while confirming that the frontend move has not widened access to customer records.

payload.content:
## [3. Decide whether the database needs to move](https://www.prisma.io#3-decide-whether-the-database-needs-to-move)

Keep a working backend initially if the app uses its authentication, storage, data API or realtime behavior. [Bolt's advanced database settings](https://support.bolt.new/bolt-cloud/database/advanced) describe claiming a Bolt database into Supabase; connecting a different database is a distinct action and can replace the existing connection. Read the current procedure before changing it.

For Lovable Cloud, follow its [backend migration sequence](https://docs.lovable.dev/tips-tricks/external-deployment-hosting#host-backend-and-data-on-a-managed-provider-supabase-example). Inventory what the export contains and what you must configure separately. Do not equate a copy of application tables with a completed migration of users, files and functions.

payload.section: [When does moving to Prisma Postgres make sense?](https://www.prisma.io#when-does-moving-to-prisma-postgres-make-sense)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host my exported Bolt or Lovable app? > [When does moving to Prisma Postgres make sense?](https://www.prisma.io#when-does-moving-to-prisma-postgres-make-sense)
payload.content:
## [When does moving to Prisma Postgres make sense?](https://www.prisma.io#when-does-moving-to-prisma-postgres-make-sense)

Move to Prisma Postgres when you want managed PostgreSQL behind a server you control, and you have accounted for the backend features the application currently uses. Prisma Compute can host that TypeScript server alongside its declared database. The browser calls your authorized server API; the server queries Postgres.

That can be a clear arrangement for an order portal: authenticate the customer, derive their account on the server, then query only that account's orders. Keep uploaded documents in [object storage](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/object-storage), with object references in Postgres. A browser SDK pointed at a hosted backend cannot be converted to this arrangement by substituting a database URL.

Choose between a [Composer database declaration](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases), which provisions its resource, and connecting a separately created database through its own configuration. With a plain Postgres dependency, your team manages migrations. For an existing database, rehearse the [Prisma Postgres import procedure](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/import-from-existing-database) against a test target first.

Check extensions, schema compatibility, ownership and grants, row counts and relationships. Prisma Postgres credentials have [full access to the database](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database#access-and-permissions), and the source database's roles do not carry over as an authorization system. If your application depends on Supabase's browser data API and RLS context, preserve that backend or redesign and test the access path before switching.

payload.content:
## [How should I switch production traffic?](https://www.prisma.io#how-should-i-switch-production-traffic)

Choose a maintenance window or a tested synchronization process so writes during the copy are accounted for. Copy and verify the final data and file objects, configure the production server secrets and auth callbacks, then change traffic only after the preview checks pass. Keep a rollback plan that accounts for writes made after the switch; pointing the domain back does not move those new records to the old database.

Price the actual arrangement: application hosting, database usage, storage and any retained builder backend. Use [Prisma pricing](https://www.prisma.io/pricing), [Netlify pricing](https://www.netlify.com/pricing/) and [Vercel pricing](https://vercel.com/pricing) to check the chosen plans rather than assuming that a code export removes every existing bill.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host my exported Bolt or Lovable app? > [When is Prisma the wrong choice?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-prisma-the-wrong-choice)
payload.content:
## [When is Prisma the wrong choice?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-prisma-the-wrong-choice)

Keep the current backend if you need its auth, storage, realtime or browser APIs and are not ready to replace them. Prisma Postgres alone does not supply those application services. Choose another runtime if a dependency cannot run under Bun, and another hosting arrangement for a WebSocket server or persistent local filesystem. Those are [Compute limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations), not build settings an assistant can wish away.

For valuable customer data, check [backup and recovery behavior](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) before cutting over. Paid Prisma plans provide daily snapshots on days with database activity; point-in-time recovery is not available. Choose a provider with the recovery guarantees your business requires if losing changes since a snapshot is unacceptable.

payload.content:
## What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)is a practical fit for an AI-built TypeScript business app because its services and database live in one project, with a Console and CLI your assistant can help inspect. You can manage routine operations as the owner, but the application still needs someone responsible for authentication, code changes and recovery.

The first question is what you expect to manage. Checking a live URL, reviewing a bill and approving a tested release are reasonable owner tasks. Diagnosing an authorization flaw or recovering corrupted business records may need experienced technical help. A managed platform removes server administration from that list, while application ownership stays with the business.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The vendor sources linked below were checked on October 20, 2026. This guide is for an existing TypeScript app; it does not assume that hosting turns custom software into a maintained business product.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [What should the platform take care of?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-the-platform-take-care-of)
payload.content:
## [What should the platform take care of?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-the-platform-take-care-of)

Look for a repeatable deployment process, an identifiable live version, accessible logs and a managed database. Keep the hosting account, source repository, domain and billing under business-controlled ownership. A contractor's personal account should not be the only route to your customer records.

Your assistant should be able to explain how the app is built, where data is saved and how a release is checked. Put the deployment declaration and migrations in the repository so future help can inspect them. Store credentials in a password manager and server-side secret configuration, with a recovery path that survives someone's departure.

payload.content:
## [Which hosting approach fits this situation?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-approach-fits-this-situation)

These app hosts are ordered alphabetically. All require you to maintain your own application code.

| Approach | Good fit | Owner's next check | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify + managed Postgres | An existing app already uses its [Git deployments and framework integration](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/deploy-overview/). | Confirm who owns the database account and how server functions receive its credentials. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | A TypeScript app whose server and database you want in one project, inspectable through [Console and CLI](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started). | Have the app's Composer declaration, environment inputs and recovery procedure explained at handoff. | 
| Vercel + managed Postgres | A Next.js app already built around [Vercel's deployment workflow](https://vercel.com/docs/deployments). | Verify access to production deployments and the separate database's backups and billing. | 

Prisma Compute gives a small team a concrete TypeScript deployment definition for its agent to read and change. Prisma Postgres accepts ordinary PostgreSQL clients, so an existing app can keep its database library. For an owner who wants a finished tool maintained by its vendor, compare a hosted business application or a supported app builder instead of starting with a custom repository.

payload.content:
## [1. Establish ownership and a release boundary](https://www.prisma.io#1-establish-ownership-and-a-release-boundary)

Use [getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started) to prepare a Composer app and a managed database. Ask whoever prepares the app to demonstrate the build, an [isolated review deployment](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/deploying#production-and-stages) using a named stage such as `--stage review`, and a separate production release. Define which changes you can approve yourself and who handles failures you cannot diagnose.

Keep reviews on [separate test data](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/typescript-test-environment). If the app receives a manually supplied database URL, configure the test and production values separately. A test deployment connected to the production database can still change customer records.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [2. Keep a short operations record](https://www.prisma.io#2-keep-a-short-operations-record)
payload.content:
## [2. Keep a short operations record](https://www.prisma.io#2-keep-a-short-operations-record)

Record the project, production branch, service name, live URL, database identity and the repository commit for the current release. Add a representative business test, such as signing in and saving a fictional booking, plus its cleanup procedure. Record where errors go and who can help; do not paste secret values into this document.

After CLI login using the current [supported runtime](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations#cli), the owner or assistant can inspect an existing project:

Here `business-portal`, `main` and `web` stand for your actual project, confirmed production branch and service name returned by the list. These commands inspect resources; they do not deploy or write customer data. The [service reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service) explains the returned live-version details. Use `@latest` deliberately for the hosting CLI; it does not require upgrading the app's installed ORM.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [3. Decide what recovery means](https://www.prisma.io#3-decide-what-recovery-means)
payload.content:
## [3. Decide what recovery means](https://www.prisma.io#3-decide-what-recovery-means)

Set a tolerable amount of lost work and a tolerable recovery time. A database snapshot from yesterday may be unacceptable if today's orders cannot be reconstructed. Prisma Postgres [backups](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) depend on the plan, and point-in-time recovery is not available until November 2026. Choose the provider and plan around the business requirement.

Rehearse restoration into a separate database and check that the application can read it. Keep exports where appropriate, and verify that the business can reach the credentials needed to recover. A backup entry in a dashboard is less useful than a restoration procedure someone has tested.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [4. Review usage and changes regularly](https://www.prisma.io#4-review-usage-and-changes-regularly)
payload.content:
## [4. Review usage and changes regularly](https://www.prisma.io#4-review-usage-and-changes-regularly)

Use the current [pricing and plan limits](https://www.prisma.io/pricing) to set a budget, and understand what happens when a limit stops service. Paid-plan spending controls and free-plan quotas protect different things; neither proves that the app will stay available under every workload.

Review failed requests, dependency updates and access changes as part of operating the app. Test updates before release and retain the previous working version and its compatible schema. The [deployment handoff guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/deployment-handoff-checks) gives a practical acceptance check.

For checks that distinguish a running process from a working customer flow, use the [app and database health guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/app-database-health-checks). It connects service inspection, bounded database checks and an external test of the public app.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting can I manage for an AI-built business app without a full-time developer? > [When is this the wrong setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-this-the-wrong-setup)
payload.content:
## [When is this the wrong setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-this-the-wrong-setup)

Choose a maintained business product if you need someone else to own both hosting and the application's ongoing behavior. An AI assistant can help with the work, but it does not create an accountable maintainer or guarantee that a proposed fix is correct.

Also check the [Compute runtime limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations). Deployed services run on Bun; WebSocket servers and a persistent writable filesystem are unsupported, and each service runs in one region. Keep Prisma Postgres with another app host when that host better fits a required runtime or operating workflow.

Before relying on the backup policy, [practice restoring a hosted Postgres database](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/practice-database-recovery) into an isolated target and verify the application against the recovered records.

## Which hosting service can Cursor help set up for my TypeScript app?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)is a strong fit when you want the TypeScript app and

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)in one project, using a deployment declaration your assistant can edit. Vercel and Netlify are also practical choices for apps already built around their framework integrations. Choose the host for your app's runtime, then let Cursor help with its setup.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)6 min read

The useful question is whether your assistant can inspect the deployment configuration, run the build and tell you what failed. A host's CLI, documented configuration files and readable logs make that work possible. Your editor does not need a special partnership with the host for its terminal to run a deployment command.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The official documentation linked below was checked on October 17, 2026. Prisma ORM is optional; choosing Prisma hosting does not require rewriting database access to use it.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [What should Cursor inspect before choosing a host?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-cursor-inspect-before-choosing-a-host)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting service can Cursor help set up for my TypeScript app? > [What should Cursor inspect before choosing a host?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-cursor-inspect-before-choosing-a-host)
payload.content:
## [What should Cursor inspect before choosing a host?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-cursor-inspect-before-choosing-a-host)

Ask Cursor to identify the framework, package manager, build command, server entry point and database client from your project. Have it report whether the app needs long-running processes, WebSocket connections, scheduled work or writable local files. These requirements decide which runtime can run the app.

It should also find where configuration comes from without printing secret values. A working local `.env` file does not configure the deployment environment. An app that uses an in-memory array or browser storage may need a [persistent database](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/prototype-customer-data) before it can support real customers.

Cursor's [Agent documentation](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/overview) describes its code editing and terminal tools. Review the proposed file changes and resource targets before authorizing commands that affect an account.

payload.content:
## [Which hosting workflows can it help with?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-workflows-can-it-help-with)

These options are ordered alphabetically by host name.

| App host | Useful project workflow | What to check first | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify | Configure the build and use its [CLI or Git deployment workflow](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/create-deploys/). | Your framework's server features must be supported by the deployment integration. A frontend upload does not deploy an arbitrary backend process. | 
| Prisma Compute | Edit the TypeScript Composer module, build the app and use the [Prisma deployment CLI](https://www.prisma.io/docs/prisma-compute/deploy). | The app must fit the deployed Bun runtime and [supported features](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations). Declare the services, database dependencies and inputs explicitly. | 
| Vercel | Link the project and use its [CLI preview deployment workflow](https://vercel.com/docs/projects/deploy-from-cli). | Confirm the framework configuration, function runtime and separate Preview and Production environment variables. | 

A Prisma Composer module is a TypeScript file that declares the app's services, database dependencies and environment inputs. Prisma Compute keeps this file alongside application code. That gives Cursor concrete files to review when a dependency or environment input changes. Prisma's [MCP server](https://www.prisma.io/docs/ai/tools/mcp-server) can also expose account resources and diagnostic tools after you authorize the connection.

Start with a bounded instruction such as:

Inspect this project's framework and runtime dependencies. Follow the current Prisma Compute deployment guide to prepare a review deployment with its own Postgres database. Show the build command, proposed resource names and environment inputs before deploying. Keep production credentials out of this environment.


Ask it to read the documentation rather than invent commands from an older CLI version. Confirm that the app's dependencies work on the deployed runtime before provisioning services.

## [2. Connect MCP if you want its tools](https://www.prisma.io#2-connect-mcp-if-you-want-its-tools)

Follow [Cursor's MCP configuration documentation](https://cursor.com/docs/mcp) and Prisma's [MCP setup guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/ai/tools/mcp-server). For a project configuration at `.cursor/mcp.json`, the hosted Prisma endpoint is:

Merge this entry into an existing configuration instead of replacing other servers. Complete the browser sign-in, select the intended workspace and approve the requested access. Keep credentials out of the JSON file. Review the tools Cursor makes available; the connected server's actual tool list determines what the assistant can do.

MCP is useful for working with resources and diagnostics. It does not replace the application build or guarantee that an arbitrary local project is ready to deploy.

payload.content:
## [3. Prepare and build the application](https://www.prisma.io#3-prepare-and-build-the-application)

Follow the [framework-specific deployment instructions](https://www.prisma.io/docs/prisma-compute/deploy) to define a Composer module, configure its inputs and produce the required artifact. Server processes must listen on the assigned service port and `0.0.0.0`. Run the app's tests and build locally before uploading it.

Declare the review database using the [Composer database dependency guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases), or supply a separately managed test database URL as a server-side input. For a declared dependency named `db`, the server receives its connection through `service.load().db.url`. Keep other secrets in server-side inputs. If you use manually configured connection strings, verify them independently: the deployment's name does not prove that its URL points to a test database.

payload.section: [4. Authenticate the CLI and deploy the review stage](https://www.prisma.io#4-authenticate-the-cli-and-deploy-the-review-stage)

payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Choose another host if required dependencies need a runtime feature outside Prisma Compute's supported environment. For example, it does not provide a persistent writable filesystem or host WebSocket servers. Customer uploads belong in object storage on any host; see [where to store files that disappear after a redeploy](https://www.prisma.io/compute/file-uploads-disappear-after-redeploy). You can still use Prisma Postgres from another application host.

If the app already deploys correctly to Netlify or Vercel, improving that configuration can be less work than migrating. Cursor can help with those CLIs too. Restricting credentials and account access matters on every host: a natural-language instruction to avoid production is useful context, but it is not an account permission boundary.

For database provisioning choices specifically, see [Postgres providers Codex can provision through tools or an API](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/codex-database-provisioning). That guide distinguishes infrastructure credentials from the application's database connection.
