payload.section: Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure?
payload.content:
## Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute), a custom domain is one CNAME on a production app, and Prisma Compute verifies the DNS record and provisions the certificate.

[Gregory Boch](https://github.com/gregory-boch-prisma)7 min read

When the generated URL (`your-app.example-host.com`) works and your own domain does not, the app itself is running. A request to your domain fails before it reaches the app, or it reaches the app with a name the app does not expect. The fix is configuration in three places: the host's domain settings, your DNS provider and the app itself.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The other providers' documentation linked on this page was checked on October 19, 2026.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [Which layer is failing?](https://www.prisma.io#which-layer-is-failing)
payload.content:
## [Which layer is failing?](https://www.prisma.io#which-layer-is-failing)

What the browser shows on your domain points to the layer to fix. Run the checks against your own hostname.

| What you see on your domain | Likely cause | Check | 
|---|---|---|
| "Site can't be reached", `NXDOMAIN` | No DNS record, or a typo in its name | `dig +short app.example.com` returns nothing | 
| A registrar parking page or an old site | An old record still answers, or the new one hasn't propagated | `dig +short app.example.com` returns an address you don't recognize | 
| A 404 page or error page from the host | DNS points at the host, but the domain isn't added to your app | The domain is missing or unverified in the host's settings | 
| A certificate warning | No certificate has been issued for your domain yet | The domain status in the host's dashboard or CLI | 
| "Too many redirects" | A proxy and the app redirect between HTTP and HTTPS | The proxy's TLS mode and the app's redirect rules | 
| The page loads, but login, API calls or sessions fail | The app still uses the old URL | Base URL, OAuth redirect URIs, CORS origins, cookie domain |

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [Why it happens](https://www.prisma.io#why-it-happens)
payload.content:
## [Why it happens](https://www.prisma.io#why-it-happens)

A hosting platform serves many apps from shared infrastructure and decides which app gets a request from the hostname in that request. Your domain only reaches your app when three things line up. DNS has to send the name to the host, the host has to know the name belongs to your app, and the host needs a TLS certificate issued for that exact name. The generated URL already has all three, which is why it works.

The fourth gap is inside the app. Code and settings written while the app lived at the generated URL often hard-code that URL. Redirects, OAuth callbacks, API calls from the browser and cookies then keep pointing at the old name.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [How to fix it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-fix-it)
payload.content:
## [How to fix it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-fix-it)

These steps work on any host. Replace `app.example.com` with your hostname and use the record values your host gives you.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [1. Add the domain in the host's settings](https://www.prisma.io#1-add-the-domain-in-the-hosts-settings)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [1. Add the domain in the host's settings](https://www.prisma.io#1-add-the-domain-in-the-hosts-settings)
payload.content:
## [1. Add the domain in the host's settings](https://www.prisma.io#1-add-the-domain-in-the-hosts-settings)

DNS alone does not attach a domain to an app. Add the exact hostname in the host's domain settings, and add `example.com` and `www.example.com` separately if you want both. [Vercel's troubleshooting guide](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/troubleshooting) starts with the same question: is the domain added to the project? Some hosts check DNS before they accept the domain, so the order of steps 1 and 2 depends on the host.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [2. Create the record the host asks for](https://www.prisma.io#2-create-the-record-the-host-asks-for)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [2. Create the record the host asks for](https://www.prisma.io#2-create-the-record-the-host-asks-for)
payload.content:
## [2. Create the record the host asks for](https://www.prisma.io#2-create-the-record-the-host-asks-for)

For a subdomain such as `app.example.com` or `www.example.com`, create a CNAME record whose value is the target the host shows. For the root domain, `example.com`, a plain CNAME isn't allowed: [RFC 1034](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1034.txt) says that when a CNAME is present at a name, no other data should be, and the root always has NS records. Use the A record the host provides, or a DNS provider that offers a CNAME-like record at the root, such as Cloudflare's [CNAME flattening](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/cname-flattening/) or an ALIAS or ANAME record.

Two mistakes are common. On providers whose Name field expects only the label (`app`), entering the full hostname creates `app.example.com.example.com`. And a retyped target with a typo, or with a trailing period dropped that the host included on purpose, can point somewhere other than the host: paste the value exactly as the host shows it. [Vercel's guide](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/troubleshooting#absolute-cname-records) covers the trailing period under absolute CNAME records.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [3. Remove conflicting records and check what resolvers see](https://www.prisma.io#3-remove-conflicting-records-and-check-what-resolvers-see)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [3. Remove conflicting records and check what resolvers see](https://www.prisma.io#3-remove-conflicting-records-and-check-what-resolvers-see)
payload.content:
## [3. Remove conflicting records and check what resolvers see](https://www.prisma.io#3-remove-conflicting-records-and-check-what-resolvers-see)

Delete old A, AAAA or CNAME records on the same name, such as a registrar's parking page or a previous host. Then check the answer from public resolvers instead of your own machine:

If the answers don't match what the host expects, the problem is still DNS. Resolvers keep an old answer until its TTL expires. [Vercel's guide](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/troubleshooting) recommends lowering the old record's TTL before a switch, and notes that nameserver changes can take up to 24 to 48 hours.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [4. Let the certificate issue, then test HTTPS](https://www.prisma.io#4-let-the-certificate-issue-then-test-https)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [4. Let the certificate issue, then test HTTPS](https://www.prisma.io#4-let-the-certificate-issue-then-test-https)
payload.content:
## [4. Let the certificate issue, then test HTTPS](https://www.prisma.io#4-let-the-certificate-issue-then-test-https)

Most hosts request a certificate for your domain automatically once DNS points at them. With the common [HTTP-01 challenge](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/challenge-types/), the certificate authority fetches a file from your domain, so issuance can't finish until step 3 is done. Check what the server returns:

If HTTP answers and HTTPS fails, the certificate isn't there yet. Two settings often block it:

- **CAA records.** A CAA record lists the certificate authorities allowed to issue for your domain. If you have CAA records, they must allow the authority your host uses. [Let's Encrypt's CAA page](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/caa/) explains the format, and `dig +short CAA example.com` shows yours.
- **A proxy in front of the host.** When Cloudflare proxies a record, lookups return [Cloudflare's addresses](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/proxy-status/) instead of your host's target, so a host that checks the record or serves the HTTP challenge may not see it. Set the record to DNS only, or follow your host's proxy instructions. If you keep the proxy, Cloudflare's Flexible mode sends plain HTTP to the host, and an app that redirects HTTP to HTTPS then [loops](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ssl/troubleshooting/too-many-redirects/). Use Full (strict) once the host has a certificate.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [5. Update the app's own settings](https://www.prisma.io#5-update-the-apps-own-settings)
payload.content:
## [5. Update the app's own settings](https://www.prisma.io#5-update-the-apps-own-settings)

When the domain loads but parts of the app fail, search the code and environment for the generated hostname and change:

- **The base URL.** Environment variables such as `APP_URL` or `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` that build links, redirects and API calls.
- **OAuth redirect URIs.** Identity providers only redirect to URIs registered with them. Google returns `redirect_uri_mismatch` when the URI [doesn't match an authorized redirect URI](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/web-server) for the client. Add the new callback URL in each provider's console.
- **CORS origins.** An API on another hostname must list the new origin in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, and requests with credentials need the exact origin rather than `*` ([MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS)).
- **Cookies.** If the app sets cookies with `Domain` set to the old hostname, browsers [reject them](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie) when the response comes from your domain. Omit `Domain` for a host-only cookie, or set it to your domain.
- **Host checks and redirects.** If your server or framework checks the `Host` header against an allowlist, add the new name. Pick one canonical hostname, for example `www` or the root, and redirect the other to it.

Redeploy after changing environment variables. Many builds read them only when the app builds or starts.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [Custom domains on Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io#custom-domains-on-prisma-compute)
payload.content:
## [Custom domains on Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io#custom-domains-on-prisma-compute)

A [custom domain](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/domains) on Prisma Compute attaches to a production app that has a promoted, running deployment. It uses one CNAME record that points at `switchboard.{region}.prisma.build`, the routing layer in front of the app. Prisma Compute verifies the DNS record, provisions the TLS certificate and terminates TLS, so there is no certificate to upload. The flow runs from the Prisma CLI:

1. Register the domain. Registration checks DNS first, so a run before the record exists fails with `DOMAIN_DNS_NOT_CONFIGURED` and prints the record name and value to create:
2. Create the printed CNAME record at your DNS provider. The CLI prints the full hostname as the record name; enter only the label (`app`) if your provider expects a relative name.
3. Once the record has propagated, run the same `add` command again. TLS provisioning starts, and `wait` polls until the domain is active, for up to 15 minutes:
4. If the domain stays in `pending_dns` or `provisioning_tls`, or ends in `failed`, inspect it, then retry stuck provisioning:

`show` prints the state, certificate details and any DNS hints. `retry` returns `DOMAIN_RETRY_NOT_ELIGIBLE` when the domain isn't in a retryable state.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [Custom domains on Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io#custom-domains-on-prisma-compute)
payload.content:
`show` prints the state, certificate details and any DNS hints. `retry` returns `DOMAIN_RETRY_NOT_ELIGIBLE` when the domain isn't in a retryable state.

The record has to resolve to the Switchboard target. The [launch post on custom domains](https://www.prisma.io/blog/prisma-compute-custom-domains) says validation accepts "either the expected CNAME target or the underlying regional records associated with that target." A record proxied through Cloudflare answers with [Cloudflare's anycast addresses](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/proxy-status/) instead, so if you use Cloudflare DNS, set the record to DNS only (gray cloud). Keeping the proxy, the other option in step 4, isn't documented for Prisma Compute.

Steps 3 and 5 of the general fix still apply, as does the CAA check in step 4: remove conflicting records, keep CAA records compatible with certificate issuance, and give the app's base URL, OAuth callbacks and cookies the new name. Environment variable values on Prisma Compute resolve at deploy time, so deploy again after you change them. Prisma Compute doesn't require Prisma ORM or Prisma Postgres, so this applies to any app you deploy there.

The limits on the [Domains page](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/domains) and [Known limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations) decide whether this setup fits:

- Custom domains attach to production apps only. Preview apps keep their generated URLs.
- DNS uses CNAME records only. A root domain needs a DNS provider with ALIAS, ANAME or CNAME flattening. Without one, put the app on a subdomain such as `www` or `app`.
- Wildcard hostnames such as `*.example.com` are rejected.
- Each service can have up to 3 custom domains.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)
payload.content:
## [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)

Lower the TTL on the existing record a day before you switch hosts, so a mistake rolls back quickly. Keep the generated URL working: it is the control that tells you whether a failure is in the app or in the domain setup. Keep the canonical URL in one environment variable rather than in code, and register OAuth callbacks for every hostname you serve before you move traffic.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Custom domain not working but the hosting URL works: what do I need to configure? > [When this fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#when-this-fix-doesnt-apply)
payload.content:
## [When this fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#when-this-fix-doesnt-apply)

If the generated URL fails too, the problem is in the app or the deployment, not the domain. Check the deploy logs first. If the domain works for you but not for some visitors, compare resolvers and networks before changing records, because a cached answer or a network that filters traffic can explain it.

Some setups need a feature a host may not offer: a wildcard domain for many tenants, a custom domain on a preview environment, or an A record at the root because your DNS provider has no CNAME flattening. Prisma Compute supports none of these today, as [the Domains page](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/domains) lists, so choose a host that does if you need one of them.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: What hosting should I use for customer reports?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports?
payload.content:
## What hosting should I use for customer reports?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute),

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)and an Object Store bucket keep those resources in one project. That is a practical fit for a TypeScript business app with bounded report requests. Keep Vercel or Netlify when their existing workflow fits, and choose a suitable worker runtime for generation that must finish independently of a request.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)6 min read

The report is useful only if the right customer can obtain the right result. That includes a saved filter choice, a defined view of the data, a generation status and a file that still exists after the next deployment.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The linked hosting, storage and PostgreSQL documentation was checked on October 22, 2026.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [What determines the hosting setup?](https://www.prisma.io#what-determines-the-hosting-setup)
payload.content:
## [What determines the hosting setup?](https://www.prisma.io#what-determines-the-hosting-setup)

Start with the actual report engine and workload. A small CSV can come from a bounded database query. A large PDF may need a rendering library, substantial memory or a browser process. Test that dependency in the intended runtime before choosing a host.

Decide whether the result must be generated during the request or can arrive later. Measure query time, rendering time, output size and concurrent requests with a representative dataset. A successful two-row demo does not establish how a customer's largest report behaves.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [Which app host fits the report endpoint?](https://www.prisma.io#which-app-host-fits-the-report-endpoint)
payload.content:
## [Which app host fits the report endpoint?](https://www.prisma.io#which-app-host-fits-the-report-endpoint)

These app hosts are listed alphabetically. Each can connect to managed Postgres and an appropriate object store.

| Setup | Useful fit | Verify before launch | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify + Prisma Postgres | An existing app built around [Netlify functions](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/overview/). | The chosen runtime supports the renderer and the report fits the function's documented limits. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres + Object Store | A TypeScript app that wants its server, database and [private files](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/object-storage) in one project. | The deployed Bun runtime supports the report engine, and longer work has a durable execution plan. | 
| Vercel + Prisma Postgres | A Next.js app already using [Vercel functions](https://vercel.com/docs/functions). | Renderer dependencies, request duration and how unfinished work is recovered. | 

For a new TypeScript app serving small customer-scoped reports, Compute keeps the endpoint and saved data together. You can also use Prisma Postgres while keeping the report API on an existing host.

payload.content:
## [1. Define the report and its customer boundary](https://www.prisma.io#1-define-the-report-and-its-customer-boundary)

Create a development Prisma Postgres database and a private [Object Store bucket](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/object-storage) in the intended project. Use fictional customer data and separate storage from production while testing.

Store a report identifier, owning account, requested filters, generation state, creation time and eventual object key. The server derives the account from verified authentication. A request's account field or an unguessable report identifier is not sufficient permission to query or download another customer's data.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [2. Check the query before adding a renderer](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-query-before-adding-a-renderer)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [2. Check the query before adding a renderer](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-query-before-adding-a-renderer)
payload.content:
## [2. Check the query before adding a renderer](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-query-before-adding-a-renderer)

With `psql` installed, open a development database connection and run this self-contained example. It reads fictional values and creates no tables:

The result is `order_count = 2` and `total_cents = 17500`. The other account is excluded. In application code, bind the authorized account as a parameter and validate report filters. The constant in this demonstration is not an authentication implementation.

Define whether a report describes current data or a saved state at a particular time. For a small report that needs several queries to agree, begin a short read-only transaction at PostgreSQL's [Repeatable Read isolation level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html#XACT-REPEATABLE-READ) before the first query. Collect the authorized inputs and commit before rendering or uploading. For large exports, design a saved or versioned input dataset rather than holding an open transaction through a long rendering job. Pagination alone does not freeze records that are being updated.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [3. Choose synchronous or queued generation](https://www.prisma.io#3-choose-synchronous-or-queued-generation)
payload.content:
## [3. Choose synchronous or queued generation](https://www.prisma.io#3-choose-synchronous-or-queued-generation)

For a bounded report, query authorized data, render it and return the result within the host's limits. Handle client disconnects and errors without reporting a completed download that never existed.

Compute has [60 seconds to start responding](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout). Streaming can continue after the first response bytes, but it does not make a generation task durable. If work must finish independently of the request, save a report job and give it a deployed worker with a reliable trigger, retry policy and recovery after interruption.

The [Postgres job-queue guide](https://www.prisma.io/blog/you-dont-need-a-job-queue-postgres-already-has-skip-locked#where-to-run-the-worker) covers worker hosting. A process that must poll while there are no visitors belongs on a suitable always-on worker host. `waitUntil` can keep a Compute instance awake for best-effort work, but it does not supply durable retries or survive every redeploy.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [4. Publish the file only after it exists](https://www.prisma.io#4-publish-the-file-only-after-it-exists)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What hosting should I use for customer reports? > [4. Publish the file only after it exists](https://www.prisma.io#4-publish-the-file-only-after-it-exists)
payload.content:
## [4. Publish the file only after it exists](https://www.prisma.io#4-publish-the-file-only-after-it-exists)

Upload the finished result to a private object key for that job attempt, then mark the report ready in Postgres with that reference. An object upload and a database transaction are separate operations. If the state update fails, retry or reconcile the saved job and object; clean up abandoned attempt files through a defined procedure.

Before issuing a download, check that the authenticated account owns the ready report. The [object storage guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/object-storage) shows presigned URLs; set a short lifetime and keep the bucket private, with credentials available only to the server.

When generating CSV from customer-entered text, handle both CSV quoting and spreadsheet interpretation of formulas. Follow [CSV injection guidance](https://community.owasp.org/attacks/CSV_Injection) for values that spreadsheet software may execute; quoting a cell does not by itself make it inert.

payload.content:
## [5. Deploy and test recovery](https://www.prisma.io#5-deploy-and-test-recovery)

Configure the server with [Compute getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started) or [Port an existing app](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/porting-an-app). Build before deploying and prepare each database with its [migrations](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/production-database-migrations). A newly declared deployment database does not inherit the Console development database's records.

Test a large report, two accounts requesting the same type, a failed upload, a worker restart and a repeated generation request. Verify that an unauthorized account cannot obtain the report and that the ready file survives an app redeploy. Put report progress and failure information in an authenticated status view.

payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Choose a worker runtime that supports the renderer when it needs dependencies outside [Compute's runtime limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations), or when generation must run as an always-on process. Compute can remain the customer-facing app while the worker uses the same managed Postgres database.

For internal analysis, an existing reporting or BI product may be more appropriate than a custom download service. For saved business data, choose the [backup and restore plan](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) separately from file delivery; a downloadable report is not a backup of the underlying database.

payload.content:
## Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)is a good fit for a TypeScript handoff because its CLI exposes services, live versions and logs, with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)available in the same project. Netlify and Vercel also expose deployment details. A successful build is one check; sign-in, database writes and the correct live version need their own checks.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)7 min read

A handoff should leave the owner able to answer three questions: which version is live, whether its server can do the business task, and where to look when that task fails. The contractor's working laptop and a green build indicator do not answer all three.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. Provider sources linked here were checked on October 19, 2026. The service commands below inspect existing resources without deploying code or changing configuration. The acceptance test in step 3 writes a fictional record in production; use an agreed test account and clean up afterward.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [What evidence should the owner be able to see?](https://www.prisma.io#what-evidence-should-the-owner-be-able-to-see)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [What evidence should the owner be able to see?](https://www.prisma.io#what-evidence-should-the-owner-be-able-to-see)
payload.content:
## [What evidence should the owner be able to see?](https://www.prisma.io#what-evidence-should-the-owner-be-able-to-see)

Ask for the repository commit, platform project, production URL and service or deployment identifier. Keep the hosting account, domain and database ownership with the business. Give the contractor the platform access their work needs, then review access at handoff.

Separate build output from runtime evidence. Build logs explain compilation and packaging; runtime logs explain requests to the running server. Neither proves by itself that a customer can log in and save the right record. Agree on an acceptance test that covers the workflow the business bought.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [Which host exposes useful deployment evidence?](https://www.prisma.io#which-host-exposes-useful-deployment-evidence)
payload.content:
## [Which host exposes useful deployment evidence?](https://www.prisma.io#which-host-exposes-useful-deployment-evidence)

These hosts are listed alphabetically. Each needs an application-level acceptance test.

| Host | What the owner can inspect | When it fits | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify | [Deploy summaries and deploy logs](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/deploy-overview/), plus [function logs](https://docs.netlify.com/manage/monitoring/logs/). | The app already uses Netlify's framework and function workflow. | 
| Prisma Compute | [Service details, live versions and version logs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service); build output is available in Console. | You want TypeScript hosting and managed Postgres in one project, with CLI inspection for the owner or their assistant. | 
| Vercel | [Deployment details and build output](https://vercel.com/docs/deployments), plus [runtime logs](https://vercel.com/docs/logs). | The Next.js app already follows Vercel's deployment workflow. | 

Keep an existing host if it already gives the owner the access and evidence they need. Prisma Postgres can remain the database from another app host; moving the frontend is optional.

payload.content:
## [1. Confirm the account, project and service](https://www.prisma.io#1-confirm-the-account-project-and-service)

Use a supported CLI runtime from the [getting-started guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started). The commands use `prisma@latest` so an older project-local CLI is not selected. The current Prisma 8 CLI is a [release candidate](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/release-status); inspecting hosting resources does not require upgrading the app's ORM.

Authenticate as the intended account, then inspect an existing project named `customer-portal`. Here `main` is the project's confirmed production branch; replace it if your project uses another branch:

Use the service name actually returned by the list. The next commands assume it is `web` and keep the same explicit branch so a similarly named preview does not confuse the handoff:

The [service reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/service) describes these outputs. `service show` identifies the live version; the version list gives history. Keep that identifier with the agreed source commit and deployment report. The commands show real account-specific values, so there is no universal successful output to paste into a checklist.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [2. Check the intended URL and version](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-intended-url-and-version)
payload.content:
## [2. Check the intended URL and version](https://www.prisma.io#2-check-the-intended-url-and-version)

Open the live service URL from its details, then the production custom domain if one is configured. Verify the expected release marker or feature and compare it with the handoff's commit and version record. A preview can work while a production domain still serves an earlier release.

For a deployment created by an assistant or CI, retain the [deploy report](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/deploy) with its resource results and URLs. Verify its outcome and the actual live version. A process starting successfully is not the same as a completed acceptance test.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [3. Run an authenticated business action](https://www.prisma.io#3-run-an-authenticated-business-action)
payload.content:
## [3. Run an authenticated business action](https://www.prisma.io#3-run-an-authenticated-business-action)

This test writes to production through the live URL. Use the agreed test account to sign in, create or update a fictional record, reload the page and confirm the saved state. Verify that an unauthorized account cannot read it. Clean up the fictional record afterward through the application's normal workflow.

For Prisma Postgres, confirm the resource the app actually connects to and that its migrations are applied. A service can deploy while pointing to an empty test database or to credentials for the wrong environment. [Secret scopes](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-app-secrets) and database identity belong in the handoff notes without recording secret values.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [4. Check failures and the recovery path](https://www.prisma.io#4-check-failures-and-the-recovery-path)
payload.content:
## [4. Check failures and the recovery path](https://www.prisma.io#4-check-failures-and-the-recovery-path)

Read runtime logs around the acceptance request. `service logs` defaults to the live version; use `--version-id` when investigating an older one. If runtime logs are unavailable for that version, retain its ID and consult Console build output or application monitoring. Avoid writing passwords, tokens or customer payloads to logs.

Agree who handles failed deploys and how to use the [rollback procedure](https://www.prisma.io/compute/roll-back-deployment). Test recovery on a review environment and check schema compatibility. Also confirm that billing, backups and the domain can be managed by someone the business retains.

When the business operates several independent apps, keep the handoff record per app. The [multiple-app hosting guide](https://www.prisma.io/compute/multiple-business-apps) covers separate projects, databases, credentials and release boundaries under shared administration.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Which hosting setup helps me verify a contractor's Next.js deployment? > [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)
payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Choose the host whose runtime and operating workflow fit the app. Prisma Compute runs deployed services on Bun and currently lacks WebSocket server support and a persistent writable filesystem. Check the [runtime limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations) before accepting dependencies that require those features.

If the owner requires a particular monitoring integration or log retention period, verify that separately. A short deploy log and a permanent application audit record serve different needs, and the handoff should state where each lives.

After accepting the release, keep an [owner operations record](https://www.prisma.io/compute/business-app-operations) with routine checks, recovery steps and a route to technical help.

payload.section: Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres?
payload.content:
## Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)is a useful starting point: declare the TypeScript service and database together, then deploy and inspect them from the same project. For a Discord Gateway bot or a Slack Socket Mode app, choose a host with a documented continuously running process, such as Render's background workers. The database can still be Prisma Postgres.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)7 min read

A support bot might receive a slash command, save a ticket and return a reference number. A moderation bot might need a continuous stream of server events. Both can use TypeScript and Postgres, but their hosting requirements differ.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The official sources linked here were checked on October 29, 2026. This guide compares hosting models; it does not assume that every library called a bot runs the same way.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [Does your bot receive HTTP requests or maintain a connection?](https://www.prisma.io#does-your-bot-receive-http-requests-or-maintain-a-connection)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [Does your bot receive HTTP requests or maintain a connection?](https://www.prisma.io#does-your-bot-receive-http-requests-or-maintain-a-connection)
payload.content:
## [Does your bot receive HTTP requests or maintain a connection?](https://www.prisma.io#does-your-bot-receive-http-requests-or-maintain-a-connection)

Start with the bot's event delivery. [Discord interactions](https://docs.discord.com/developers/interactions/receiving-and-responding) can arrive through an HTTP endpoint or the Gateway. Those are alternative delivery methods for interactions. Receiving application commands over HTTP does not provide every Gateway event.

Slack's [HTTP Events API](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/) sends requests to your server, while [Socket Mode](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/using-socket-mode/) establishes an outbound WebSocket connection. Socket Mode needs connection refresh and reconnect handling, even when no user is issuing a command.

Inspect the library configuration with your coding assistant. A public request URL and an HTTP handler point toward a web service. Gateway login, heartbeats or a Socket Mode client point toward a continuously running process. A TypeScript runtime match by itself does not establish that the host will keep that process connected.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [Which hosting setup fits that model?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-setup-fits-that-model)
payload.content:
## [Which hosting setup fits that model?](https://www.prisma.io#which-hosting-setup-fits-that-model)

These options are ordered alphabetically by app host. Each can be paired with an external managed Postgres database; choose the service type before comparing its price.

| App host | When it fits | What to check | 
|---|---|---|
| Prisma Compute | A TypeScript HTTP bot whose service and database should be declared and deployed in one project. | The deployed runtime is Bun. Compute focuses on HTTP services; keep-awake work is best effort, and there is no persistent writable filesystem or WebSocket server support. See [limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations). | 
| [Render](https://render.com/docs/background-workers) | A Gateway or Socket Mode bot that needs a continuously running background worker, or a separate HTTP web service. | Select the worker or web-service type deliberately. Configure reconnects, shutdown behavior, server-side database access and the service's region. | 
| [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/functions) | HTTP commands that belong in an existing supported web app. | Function execution and connection lifetimes apply. For a continuous process, evaluate its separate [Daemons](https://vercel.com/docs/daemons) offering and current availability rather than assuming a Function is a permanent worker. | 

Prisma Compute fits the HTTP case especially well when a small team wants its assistant to see the service, database dependency and deployment configuration together. [Composer's plain Postgres dependency](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases) supplies connection configuration for the client you choose; adopting Prisma ORM is optional.

payload.content: For a connected bot, Render's [outbound WebSocket support](https://render.com/docs/websocket) and continuously running worker model are directly relevant. Keep important state in Postgres there too: a worker restart still replaces the process.

payload.content: ## [How should I set up the HTTP bot on Prisma?](https://www.prisma.io#how-should-i-set-up-the-http-bot-on-prisma)

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [1. Create a separate development application](https://www.prisma.io#1-create-a-separate-development-application)
payload.content:
## [1. Create a separate development application](https://www.prisma.io#1-create-a-separate-development-application)

Use a development Discord application or Slack app installation and a test channel. Store its tokens and signing configuration as [server-side environment variables](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/environment-variables). Keep production credentials out of preview environments and build output.

Deploy a TypeScript HTTP service using [Composer getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/getting-started) or [porting an existing app](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/porting-an-app). Verify the bot SDK and its HTTP adapter under Bun before connecting a live workspace.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [2. Declare one database provisioning path](https://www.prisma.io#2-declare-one-database-provisioning-path)
payload.content:
## [2. Declare one database provisioning path](https://www.prisma.io#2-declare-one-database-provisioning-path)

Declare a [plain Postgres dependency](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases) if Composer should provision the database with the service. If you already created a database separately, configure that existing connection instead. Creating both does not make them the same database.

For a separately hosted bot, obtain Prisma Postgres's [pooled connection string](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database) for application traffic and keep it on the server. Use the direct connection for migrations and administrative tools. Place the bot near its database; the [region-selection guide](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/nodejs-database-regions) explains how extra round trips affect request time.

Store installation identifiers, application records and processing state in tables. Include the workspace or server boundary in queries, so a command from one customer cannot read another customer's records.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [3. Verify the sender before accepting work](https://www.prisma.io#3-verify-the-sender-before-accepting-work)
payload.content:
## [3. Verify the sender before accepting work](https://www.prisma.io#3-verify-the-sender-before-accepting-work)

Use the platform's documented verification procedure. Discord requires verification of the request signature and a valid response to its endpoint check. Slack's [request verification](https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/verifying-requests-from-slack/) uses its signing secret and timestamp. Preserve the raw request body where the verifier requires it.

For Slack's HTTP Events API, implement the [URL-verification handshake](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/using-http-request-urls/) too. For a `url_verification` setup request, verify the request and return HTTP 200 with its `challenge` value so Slack accepts the Request URL. This handshake applies to Events API URLs, not slash-command URLs.

A valid signature establishes the sender; your handler must still check whether the installation and user may perform the requested action. Avoid logging tokens, request signatures or private message bodies merely to prove that a request arrived.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [4. Acknowledge promptly and persist work that must finish](https://www.prisma.io#4-acknowledge-promptly-and-persist-work-that-must-finish)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [4. Acknowledge promptly and persist work that must finish](https://www.prisma.io#4-acknowledge-promptly-and-persist-work-that-must-finish)
payload.content:
## [4. Acknowledge promptly and persist work that must finish](https://www.prisma.io#4-acknowledge-promptly-and-persist-work-that-must-finish)

Discord requires an initial interaction response within three seconds. Slack [interactive requests](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/handling-user-interaction/) also require acknowledgment within three seconds. Implement the appropriate response or deferral before waiting for a slow model call or report generation; do not copy a generic HTTP acknowledgment across different interaction types.

For work that must finish, commit a job or queue message before acknowledging receipt, and ensure that storage step fits the platform's deadline. For a database inbox, use a stable delivery identifier where the platform provides one, such as a Discord interaction ID or a Slack Events API event ID. Namespace it by platform and installation, require every part of that key, and enforce a [database uniqueness constraint](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-UNIQUE-CONSTRAINTS). Accept the delivery and create its pending job in one transaction, handling a uniqueness conflict atomically so concurrent retries cannot both create a job. Different command types can require a different deduplication strategy.

Arrange an explicit processor that resumes pending work. On Compute, [persisting work and processing it in steps](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout) needs a separate trigger, such as an external scheduler, Composer's cron building block or a worker elsewhere. `waitUntil` can keep an instance awake after a response; it does not supply retries or guarantee completion through a restart.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [4. Acknowledge promptly and persist work that must finish](https://www.prisma.io#4-acknowledge-promptly-and-persist-work-that-must-finish)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [4. Acknowledge promptly and persist work that must finish](https://www.prisma.io#4-acknowledge-promptly-and-persist-work-that-must-finish)
payload.content:
Plan how a resumed job delivers its result. [Discord interaction tokens](https://docs.discord.com/developers/interactions/receiving-and-responding) are valid for 15 minutes, while Slack's [`response_url` replies](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/handling-user-interaction/#message_responses) are limited to 30 minutes after receipt. If work can outlast that window, including after an outage, use an authenticated status page or a new bot message where the app has permission. Preserve the original recipient and privacy requirements rather than posting a private result to a public channel.

That uniqueness constraint prevents duplicate acceptance, but it cannot by itself make an external message send happen exactly once. Save progress, use downstream idempotency facilities where available, and decide how to reconcile a crash between sending a message and recording success.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [5. Test through the real platform](https://www.prisma.io#5-test-through-the-real-platform)
payload.content:
## [5. Test through the real platform](https://www.prisma.io#5-test-through-the-real-platform)

Send a command from the development installation and confirm the expected database change. Then repeat the delivery, restart the service during processing, and verify that pending work resumes without creating a second ticket. Check that an invalid signature is rejected and that one customer's command cannot access another customer's records.

With [deploy on push](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/deploy-on-push), declared databases receive separate resources on preview branches. Check the bot installation and platform callback configuration separately: database isolation does not redirect production Slack or Discord traffic to a test workspace.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [What should I budget for?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-i-budget-for)
payload.content:
## [What should I budget for?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-i-budget-for)

Account for the HTTP service or continuously running worker, Postgres usage and storage, and any external queue or AI API. A connected bot can consume resources while waiting for events. Repeated deliveries and retries can also add database and model calls.

Use the current [Prisma pricing](https://www.prisma.io/pricing), [Render pricing](https://render.com/pricing) or [Vercel pricing](https://vercel.com/pricing) for the service type you selected. Measure a representative command and its retry path before estimating from the number of chat users.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a TypeScript bot with Postgres? > [When is Prisma the wrong choice?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-prisma-the-wrong-choice)
payload.content:
## [When is Prisma the wrong choice?](https://www.prisma.io#when-is-prisma-the-wrong-choice)

Choose a documented continuous-worker service for a Gateway or Socket Mode bot rather than relying on an HTTP instance remaining connected indefinitely. Prisma Compute has [no WebSocket server support or persistent filesystem](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations), and its keep-awake primitives do not guarantee continuity through deployments. Keep bot state outside the process regardless of the host.

Prisma Postgres credentials have [full access to their database](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database#access-and-permissions); a separate password does not restrict a bot to one table or customer. Enforce application authorization, or choose a database setup with the restricted roles your design needs. For recovery, [paid-plan daily snapshots](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) are not point-in-time recovery. Include that distinction when choosing how to protect valuable bot records.

payload.section: Files uploaded to my Node app disappear after a redeploy. Where should I store them?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Files uploaded to my Node app disappear after a redeploy. Where should I store them?
payload.content:
## Files uploaded to my Node app disappear after a redeploy. Where should I store them?

`uploads/` folder, is gone after the next deploy or restart. Store customer uploads in S3-compatible object storage (AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, or the bucket service your host offers) and save each file's key, owner and type in your database. A persistent disk or volume also works, but each one belongs to a single instance, so the app either runs as one instance or ends up with files split across instances. On [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute), which has no persistent filesystem, uploads go to an

[Object Store bucket](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/object-storage)in the same Prisma project as your database.

[Gregory Boch](https://github.com/gregory-boch-prisma)8 min read

If customer uploads were there yesterday and are missing after a deploy, your app is almost certainly writing them to the server's local disk. On most hosting platforms that disk belongs to one running copy of your build, and the next deploy replaces it with a new one.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. Every host behavior on this page links to that host's documentation, checked on October 19, 2026. The fix works for any Node.js app, whichever framework, host or database client you use.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Files uploaded to my Node app disappear after a redeploy. Where should I store them? > [Why uploaded files disappear](https://www.prisma.io#why-uploaded-files-disappear)
payload.content:
## [Why uploaded files disappear](https://www.prisma.io#why-uploaded-files-disappear)

A deploy builds your code into an image, starts new instances from it and stops the old ones. Each new instance starts with the files from the build and nothing else, so a file your app saved at runtime, for example with multer's `diskStorage` or `fs.writeFile("./uploads/...")`, is not in it.

Hosts document this in their own words:

| Host | What happens to files your app writes at runtime | 
|---|---|
| Fly.io | A Machine's root filesystem is ephemeral, meant for data that can be rebuilt on deploys and restarts. A Fly Volume keeps files, attached to one Machine. [Docs](https://docs.fly.io/volumes/overview) | 
| Heroku | Each dyno gets a fresh copy of the latest deploy, and files it writes are discarded when it stops or restarts. Dynos restart daily. [Docs](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/dynos#ephemeral-filesystem), [S3 guide](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/s3) | 
| Prisma Compute | No persistent filesystem. Files you keep go to an Object Store bucket or the database. [Docs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations#runtime), [FAQ](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/faq) | 
| Railway | Files persist inside a mounted volume, one volume per service. Data written to the volume path at build time is not kept. [Docs](https://docs.railway.com/volumes/reference), [guide](https://docs.railway.com/volumes) | 
| Render | Changes to a service's local files are lost on every redeploy or restart, unless they are on a persistent disk. [Docs](https://render.com/docs/disks) | 
| Vercel | Functions have a read-only filesystem with a writable `/tmp` of up to 500 MB, for scratch space only. [Docs](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/runtimes#file-system-support) |

payload.content:
| Vercel | Functions have a read-only filesystem with a writable `/tmp` of up to 500 MB, for scratch space only. [Docs](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/runtimes#file-system-support) | 

Two related symptoms have the same cause. If you run more than one instance, an upload saved by one instance is missing when a request lands on another. And if uploads work on your laptop but not after deploying, that is because your laptop keeps the same disk between runs and a deployed instance doesn't.

payload.content:
## [Fix: move uploads to object storage](https://www.prisma.io#fix-move-uploads-to-object-storage)

Object storage keeps files outside your app's instances, so deploys, restarts and extra instances no longer affect them. Use any S3-compatible service: [AWS S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html), [Cloudflare R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/), [Railway Buckets](https://docs.railway.com/storage-buckets), a [Prisma Object Store bucket](https://www.prisma.io/docs/storage), or the one your host recommends. Your database then keeps one row per file, so the app can list a customer's files, check who owns a file and find it in the bucket.

## [3. Write uploads to the bucket instead of the disk](https://www.prisma.io#3-write-uploads-to-the-bucket-instead-of-the-disk)

Install the packages the example uses:

This Express example keeps the upload in memory with multer, writes it to the bucket, records it in Postgres and serves it back through a presigned URL. It uses ES modules, so save it as `server.mjs` or set `"type": "module"` in `package.json`. Replace the `ownerId` lines with your own authentication.

Generate the key yourself instead of using the customer's file name, so two files called `invoice.pdf` don't overwrite each other and nobody can write outside their own prefix. For large files such as videos, you can skip the app server: your app creates a presigned PUT URL and the browser uploads straight to the bucket. payload.content:
## [Storing uploads with Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io#storing-uploads-with-prisma-compute-and-prisma-postgres)

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) has no persistent filesystem, so the local `uploads/` folder from the start of this page doesn't work there either. Its storage option is an Object Store bucket: S3-compatible storage that lives in the same Prisma project as your [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres) database, managed from the Console, the CLI or the REST API.

To run the Express example above on Compute, deploy it as a [Prisma Composer](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer) service, which is how apps deploy to Compute. Declare the service with `compute()` and two dependencies from `@prisma/composer-prisma-cloud`, `store: bucket()` and `db: rawPostgres()`, then provision both in your `module.ts`:

Provisioning the bucket also mints its access key, so there are no storage credentials to copy. The server code changes in three places, following [porting an app](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/porting-an-app) and [object storage in Composer](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/object-storage):

Your build has to produce a self-contained entry file, and `npx prisma dev` runs the app locally against a stand-in bucket and database; [porting an app](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/porting-an-app) covers the build and the `service.ts` declaration. The `uploads` table goes in the provisioned Prisma Postgres database. To keep an existing Postgres database instead, pass its connection string as a secret [service input](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/service-input) rather than declaring `rawPostgres()`. Prisma ORM is optional either way: the example uses the `pg` driver.

payload.section: [Storing uploads with Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io#storing-uploads-with-prisma-compute-and-prisma-postgres)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Files uploaded to my Node app disappear after a redeploy. Where should I store them? > [Storing uploads with Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io#storing-uploads-with-prisma-compute-and-prisma-postgres)
payload.content:
The [object storage guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/object-storage) shows the other route: create the bucket and a key yourself, store the four values as environment variables, and read them with Bun's built-in S3 client (`Bun.s3`), which picks up these names without configuration:

`bucket key create` mints a `read_write` key unless you pass `--role read`. Its secret is shown once, so copy it right away. A deployment that only serves files can hold a `read` key, but a write with a `read` key fails with `AccessDenied`. Values resolve at deploy time, so set them before you deploy.

Things to know before you rely on it:

- **Object Store pricing and plan limits are not published yet.** The Free plan's 2 GB is Prisma Postgres database storage, which holds the `uploads` table, not the files; [pricing](https://www.prisma.io/pricing) has the other plans.
- **Deleting a bucket deletes its files and keys in one step**, even when it isn't empty, and can't be undone.
- **Requests have 60 seconds to start responding.** An upload that passes through your app has to finish arriving before your handler can respond, so it has to fit in that window; see [request timeout](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout).

payload.content:
## [How to prevent it, and when the fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it-and-when-the-fix-doesnt-apply)

Treat every instance's disk as temporary from the start. Write uploads, generated files and anything else customers expect to find again to object storage or the database, and keep local disk for scratch files that a single request creates and deletes. A test that deploys twice and checks an uploaded file between deploys catches a regression before customers do.

Object storage is the wrong fit when your app or a tool it depends on needs a real filesystem that persists: a SQLite database file, a CMS that writes its media folder to disk, or software that expects POSIX file locking. Use a host with persistent disks or volumes for those, accept that the app runs as a single instance, and back the disk up. Prisma Compute doesn't offer persistent disks, so it is the wrong host for that kind of app. [Moving SQLite data to Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/app-data-lost-after-restart) solves the database part of the problem, because the data then lives outside the instance.

payload.content:
## Frequently asked questions

`bytea` column, which keeps everything in one place, but every upload then makes the database and its backups larger and every download goes through a database query. For customer uploads such as photos, PDFs and CSVs, put the file in object storage and keep a row in Postgres with its key, owner, name, type and size.
[Render disks](https://render.com/docs/disks),

[Railway volumes](https://docs.railway.com/volumes/reference)and

[Fly Volumes](https://docs.fly.io/volumes/overview)keep files across deploys, but each is attached to a single instance: Render can't scale a service with a disk to more instances, Railway can't use replicas with a volume, and a Fly Volume attaches to one Machine. Render and Railway also note a short downtime on each deploy of a service with a disk or volume. Object storage isn't tied to an instance, so it avoids these trade-offs.

[Heroku](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/dynos#ephemeral-filesystem), for example, discards files a dyno wrote as soon as it stops or restarts. Check whether copies exist elsewhere: a CDN cache, an email attachment, a backup job or the customer's own device. Files written since the last deploy or restart may still be on the running instance, so copy them to the bucket before you deploy again.

## What does my TypeScript app need before I put it into public use?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)fits a TypeScript app you want hosted with its database in one project. Vercel and Netlify are good choices when the app already follows their framework deployment workflow. Treat the move from

`npm run dev` as an application-readiness check as well as a hosting decision.
[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)6 min read

`npm run dev` runs whatever your project's `dev` script defines. In many frameworks it starts a development server with fast rebuilds and development diagnostics. Opening that process to the internet does not establish a production deployment or prove that the application's data and access rules are ready.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. Provider and framework documentation linked here was checked on October 20, 2026. The steps apply to an existing app; use the framework's production instructions for its actual build and startup commands.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > What does my TypeScript app need before I put it into public use? > [What changes between development and production?](https://www.prisma.io#what-changes-between-development-and-production)
payload.content:
## [What changes between development and production?](https://www.prisma.io#what-changes-between-development-and-production)

The hosting provider needs an artifact it can reproduce and a supported way to run the server. Your users need the application to retain data, enforce access rules and fail in a way someone can diagnose. These are separate checks: a correct build can still point at the wrong database.

| Development assumption | Production question | 
|---|---|
| The app reads a local `.env` file. | Which server-side inputs does the deployed version receive? | 
| Test records live in memory or a local JSON file. | Which managed database stores records across instances and deploys? | 
| A developer opens the home page. | Can a real role sign in, complete the business action and see the saved result? | 
| An error appears in the terminal. | Where can the owner find a request error and the deployed version? | 
| The developer restarts the process. | How does the team recover code and data after a failed change? |

payload.content:
## [Which host should I choose?](https://www.prisma.io#which-host-should-i-choose)

Choose around the framework and runtime you actually have. The options below are listed alphabetically.

| Host | Good fit | Preparation | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify | Your framework's production integration fits Netlify's [deploy workflow](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/deploy-overview/). | Configure its build, server functions and database environment. | 
| Prisma Compute | Your TypeScript server fits the deployed Bun runtime and you want managed Postgres in the same project. | Add a [Composer declaration](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer), configure inputs and build before deploying. | 
| Vercel | Your app already follows its [framework and deployment workflow](https://vercel.com/docs/deployments). | Confirm dynamic routes, functions and the Preview/Production configuration. | 

A static export can suit an app with no server-side work. An application with private database queries or secret API calls needs those operations on a supported server runtime. Uploading a frontend folder alone does not deploy an arbitrary backend process.

## [1. Identify and run the production build](https://www.prisma.io#1-identify-and-run-the-production-build)

Read the scripts in `package.json` and the framework's deployment guide. For Next.js, review the [production checklist](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/production-checklist). For a project that uses npm, commits `package-lock.json` and defines its production build as `build`, verify a clean installation and build:

A successful command exits with code `0`; its messages depend on the application. Fix missing configuration and type/build errors before deploying. Use your repository's actual package manager and lockfile rather than introducing npm into a pnpm or Bun project.

Follow the [framework deployment guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/prisma-compute/deploy) to declare the service's build and entry point in Composer. Create an account-owned Prisma Postgres database in [Console](https://console.prisma.io), then configure the existing client with the [pooled application URL](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database). Use a separate direct connection where your migration or administration workflow requires one. Prisma ORM is optional.

## [3. Deploy a review version and exercise it](https://www.prisma.io#3-deploy-a-review-version-and-exercise-it)

Use [getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/getting-started) to authenticate, then deploy the built Composer app to a [named test stage](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/deploying#production-and-stages): `npx prisma@latest deploy --stage review`. Verify the intended project and review stage in the deploy report. Open its actual URL from a second browser or device. Test both an allowed action and an action the current user must not be allowed to perform.

## [4. Define the release and recovery procedure](https://www.prisma.io#4-define-the-release-and-recovery-procedure)

Record which source commit and live service version passed review. Keep the test steps with the repository and decide how schema changes reach production. With [deploy on push](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/deploy-on-push), the GitHub connection and the repository workflow are both required.

After review passes, check the intended production database and migration plan, then build and deploy the approved commit with production inputs. Verify the production URL and sign-in, and test a fictional save/read using an agreed test account with cleanup afterward.

Before customers depend on saved data, choose an appropriate [backup plan](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) and test restoration into a separate database. Keep code rollback and data recovery as separate procedures. Review [usage limits and spending controls](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-hosting-spending-controls) before sharing the production URL.

Prisma Compute runs deployed services on Bun and currently has no WebSocket server support, multi-region service deployment or persistent writable filesystem. Check the [runtime limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations) before committing to dependencies that require them. Prisma Postgres can still be the database from another app host.

If the remaining work is an unresolved authorization rule, missing recovery plan or unreliable business action, changing the host alone will not complete it. Resolve those application requirements in the review environment before inviting customers.

## My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run?

`waitUntil` or Next.js `after()` on Vercel. That limit is 5 minutes by default on Vercel and at most 15 minutes for a standard AWS Lambda function. Move the job out of the request: the handler saves the job and returns `202`, and something without that limit runs it. That is either a worker process on a host that keeps it running (Railway, Render or Fly.io) reading from a queue such as pg-boss or Graphile Worker on Postgres or BullMQ on Redis, or a durable workflow service such as Inngest, Trigger.dev, Vercel Workflows or Upstash Workflow that runs the job as retried steps. Whichever you pick, make every step safe to run twice. On [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute),

`waitUntil` keeps the instance awake after the response until the job's promise settles, on a best-effort basis, so the job belongs in the database as well.
Every serverless function invocation has a time limit. When the invocation reaches it, the platform stops it, and everything it started stops with it: the promise you didn't await, the loop over 10,000 rows, the call to a model API that was halfway through. Often nothing is logged except the timeout, and the work has to start over from the beginning, if anything starts it again at all. The fix is to stop running the job inside the request: save it, return `202`, and run it in a worker process on a host that keeps it running, or in a durable workflow service that retries each step.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The fix below works on any host. Platform and library behaviors on this page link to their documentation, checked on October 22, 2026.

payload.section: [Why the job stops at the time limit](https://www.prisma.io#why-the-job-stops-at-the-time-limit)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [Why the job stops at the time limit](https://www.prisma.io#why-the-job-stops-at-the-time-limit)
payload.content:
## [Why the job stops at the time limit](https://www.prisma.io#why-the-job-stops-at-the-time-limit)

Each platform sets a hard limit on how long one invocation can run. On AWS Lambda and Vercel, work you start after sending the response is bound by that same invocation.

| Platform | Time limit per invocation | Work after the response | 
|---|---|---|
| AWS Lambda | 3 seconds by default, configurable up to 900 seconds (15 minutes). Lambda Managed Instances allow up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event-source invocations. [Docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html) | Background work that hasn't finished when the handler returns is frozen with the execution environment, and resumes only if Lambda reuses that environment. [Docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtime-environment.html) | 
| Netlify | 60 seconds for synchronous functions, not configurable. Background functions run up to 15 minutes. [Configuration](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/configuration/), [background functions](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/background-functions/) | `context.waitUntil()` extends the function's execution until the promise completes, so the work still has to finish within the function's limit. [Functions API](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/api/#waituntil). A background function that returns an error is retried after 1 minute, then after 2 more. |

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [Why the job stops at the time limit](https://www.prisma.io#why-the-job-stops-at-the-time-limit)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [Why the job stops at the time limit](https://www.prisma.io#why-the-job-stops-at-the-time-limit)
payload.content:
| Prisma Compute | 60 seconds to start responding. A response that has started streaming isn't cut off. [Docs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout) | `waitUntil` keeps the instance awake until the promise settles, best effort: no retry, and no continuity through a restart or deployment. [Docs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/keeping-instances-awake) | 
| Vercel | 300 seconds by default with Fluid compute. Pro and Enterprise can raise it to 800 seconds, and to 1,800 seconds per function in a beta for Node.js, Bun and Python. Hobby stays at 300. [Limits](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration), [configuring duration](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/configuring-functions/duration) | Promises passed to `waitUntil` have the same timeout as the function, and are cancelled when it times out. [Docs](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/functions-api-reference/vercel-functions-package) | 

Raising the limit helps when a job has a known upper bound below the platform's maximum. It doesn't help when the job's length depends on the data (an import that grows with the customer's file), and it doesn't add retries. The fix is to stop tying the job to a request at all.

payload.content:
## [Fix: save the job, return, and run it somewhere else](https://www.prisma.io#fix-save-the-job-return-and-run-it-somewhere-else)

The pattern is the same on every platform. The request handler checks the input, saves a job that describes the work, and returns `202 Accepted` with the job's id. A separate process picks the job up, runs it, retries it when it fails, and records its progress where your app can read it.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [1. Pick where the job runs](https://www.prisma.io#1-pick-where-the-job-runs)
payload.content:
## [1. Pick where the job runs](https://www.prisma.io#1-pick-where-the-job-runs)

The choice is mostly about what you are willing to host and how long one job runs.

| Option | Examples | How it gets past the time limit | Choose it when | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Durable workflow service | [Inngest](https://www.inngest.com/docs/usage-limits/inngest), [Trigger.dev](https://trigger.dev/docs/runs/max-duration), [Upstash Workflow](https://upstash.com/docs/workflow/getstarted), [Vercel Workflows](https://vercel.com/docs/workflows) | Trigger.dev builds and deploys your task code to its own infrastructure and runs it there, so your host's time limit doesn't apply ( [how it works](https://trigger.dev/docs/how-it-works)). Runs have no maximum duration: you set a project default `maxDuration`, which caps each attempt's CPU time, and `timeout.None` removes the cap. Inngest, Upstash Workflow and Vercel Workflows call your own functions for each step and save each finished step, so a failed step is retried without rerunning the others, but every step must still fit your host's limit ([Inngest retries](https://www.inngest.com/docs/features/inngest-functions/error-retries/retries)). Upstash runs each step as a separate request to your app, and an Inngest step can run up to 2 hours, but no longer than your host's own timeout. | You don't want to host a worker, or the job waits on webhooks, approvals or sleeps. |

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [1. Pick where the job runs](https://www.prisma.io#1-pick-where-the-job-runs)
payload.content:
| Durable functions on your cloud | [AWS Lambda durable functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/durable-functions.html), [AWS Step Functions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/service-quotas.html) | Lambda checkpoints each step and resumes from the last checkpoint, and a durable function can run for up to one year. A Step Functions Standard workflow execution can also run up to 1 year; an Express workflow is capped at 5 minutes. | You are already on AWS. | 
| Queue in Postgres, plus a worker process | [pg-boss](https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss), [Graphile Worker](https://worker.graphile.org/docs/requirements) | Jobs are rows in your database. A long-running worker claims them with `SKIP LOCKED`, so the job runs in a process with no request attached. | You already use Postgres and want jobs to commit in the same transaction as the data they belong to. | 
| Queue in Redis, plus a worker process | [BullMQ](https://docs.bullmq.io/) | The same pattern, with Redis as the queue store. | You already run Redis, or you want BullMQ's rate limiting and priorities. | 
| Workflow engine with your own workers | [Temporal](https://docs.temporal.io/workers) | The Temporal Service keeps each workflow's state and hands out tasks. Your code runs in worker processes that you operate. | The job is a long, multi-step workflow and you are prepared to operate the workers. |

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [1. Pick where the job runs](https://www.prisma.io#1-pick-where-the-job-runs)
payload.content:
| Batch job | [Cloud Run jobs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/task-timeout), [Amazon ECS standalone tasks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/standalone-tasks.html) | Each task runs in a container that does the work and then stops. A Cloud Run task has its own timeout: 10 minutes by default, configurable up to 168 hours. On AWS, an ECS task on Fargate or your own EC2 instances fits a batch process the same way. | The job is heavy computation that needs a container image or runs for hours. | 

A worker process needs a host that keeps it running. On [Railway](https://docs.railway.com/guides/bullmq-jobs-retry-dlq), that is an always-on service in the same project, with serverless left off. On [Render](https://render.com/docs/background-workers), it is a background worker, which runs continuously and receives no network traffic; background workers don't have a free instance type ([Render free tier](https://render.com/docs/free)). On [Fly.io](https://docs.fly.io/launch/processes), it is a `worker` process group in the same app. List only the `web` group in the `processes` of your `http_service` (or `[[services]]`) section, so Fly Proxy sends requests only to the web process.

If you can't add any of these yet, split the job into chunks that each finish inside one invocation, record where each chunk ended, and have each one queue the next. It needs no new infrastructure, but every chunk is still bound by the time limit.
