payload.content:
## [2. Save the job and return](https://www.prisma.io#2-save-the-job-and-return)

The rest of this guide uses [pg-boss](https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss) on Postgres, because it needs no service besides the database you already have. It requires Node.js 22.12 or newer (or Bun) and PostgreSQL 13 or newer. The example uses ES modules, so set `"type": "module"` in `package.json`.

Create the queue in one shared module. Each process (your web app and the worker) gets its own pg-boss instance, created once and reused:

The request handler only sends the job. This one is a Next.js route handler in a project with a `src` directory, and the same three lines work in any framework:

The route queues work on the caller's behalf, so check who is calling first, the same way your other routes do: authenticate the request and confirm the caller can access `reportId`. The example leaves that check out because it depends on your auth setup.

pg-boss creates its tables in a `pgboss` schema the first time `start()` runs. Because the job is a row in your database, you can also send it inside the transaction that creates the report, so the job exists only if the report does ([pg-boss adapters](https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss/blob/master/docs/api/adapters.md)).

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [3. Run the worker as its own process](https://www.prisma.io#3-run-the-worker-as-its-own-process)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [3. Run the worker as its own process](https://www.prisma.io#3-run-the-worker-as-its-own-process)
payload.content:
## [3. Run the worker as its own process](https://www.prisma.io#3-run-the-worker-as-its-own-process)

The worker is a long-running script, not a route. It polls the queue (every 2 seconds by default), runs each job and marks it done or failed:

Run it with `npx tsx src/worker.ts` locally, and deploy it as a second service from the same repository with that start command. On a deploy, the host sends `SIGTERM` and then kills the process after a grace period. `boss.stop()` waits up to 30 seconds by default for active jobs, then fails them so they retry ([pg-boss stop](https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss/blob/master/docs/api/ops.md)). Set its `timeout` just under your host's grace period: Railway gives 0 seconds unless you set a draining time ([Railway guide](https://docs.railway.com/guides/bullmq-jobs-retry-dlq)), Render 30 seconds by default and up to 300 ([Render deploys](https://render.com/docs/deploys)), and Fly.io's `kill_timeout` 5 seconds by default and up to 300 ([Fly.io configuration](https://fly.io/docs/reference/configuration/)). A job longer than that is interrupted on every deploy, so it depends on the recorded steps in step 4. A process killed before `stop()` fails its jobs leaves them active until `expireInSeconds` passes (or the heartbeat check below notices), then pg-boss retries them.

`expireInSeconds` defaults to 15 minutes and can be at most 24 hours. Set it above the longest a job should ever take. For long jobs, also set `heartbeatSeconds` on the queue: the worker then reports that it is alive, and pg-boss notices a dead worker within `heartbeatSeconds` plus up to 60 seconds and retries its job, instead of waiting out the expiration ([pg-boss queues](https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss/blob/master/docs/api/queues.md)).

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [4. Make each job safe to run twice](https://www.prisma.io#4-make-each-job-safe-to-run-twice)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [4. Make each job safe to run twice](https://www.prisma.io#4-make-each-job-safe-to-run-twice)
payload.content:
## [4. Make each job safe to run twice](https://www.prisma.io#4-make-each-job-safe-to-run-twice)

Plan for every job to run more than once. A worker can finish the work and crash before recording it, and a step can time out after its side effect happened. BullMQ documents at-least-once delivery as the worst case ([BullMQ](https://docs.bullmq.io/)), Upstash Workflow promises at-least-once delivery ([Upstash Workflow](https://upstash.com/docs/workflow/getstarted)), and pg-boss warns that a job that expired may already be running again elsewhere ([pg-boss workers](https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss/blob/master/docs/api/workers.md)). Design for it:

- Give each side effect a key and check it before acting: a row in a `sent_emails` table, or an idempotency key passed to the payment or email API.
- Split the job into steps and record each finished step, for example the last row offset of an import. A retry starts from the last recorded step, and only the interrupted step runs again.
- Put a timeout on every network call inside the job, shorter than the job's own expiration, so one stuck request doesn't hold the whole job until it expires.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [5. Show progress to the user](https://www.prisma.io#5-show-progress-to-the-user)
payload.content:
## [5. Show progress to the user](https://www.prisma.io#5-show-progress-to-the-user)

The request returned a job id, so the page can ask for the job's state instead of holding a request open. Store status and progress in your own table (`reports.status`, `reports.progress`) and update it from the worker. The page then polls an endpoint that reads that row, or listens on a stream you send from it. pg-boss also keeps its own record of each job, which `getJobById` returns, but your table is the one your app's permissions already cover.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)
payload.content:
## [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) hosts TypeScript apps built for Node.js, Bun or Next.js; deployed apps run on Bun. Prisma Compute fits when the job is bounded and a lost run can be started again: the request saves the job in Postgres and returns within the 60-second response limit, and `waitUntil` from `@prisma/compute` keeps the instance awake until the work's promise settles ([Request timeout](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/request-timeout)). The docs describe this as bounded, best-effort background work, and an idle app scales to zero again once it finishes ([Keeping instances awake](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/keeping-instances-awake)).

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)
payload.content:
Keep the job in [Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres), in the same project as the app. If a deploy or restart interrupts the work, the job is still there, and the next trigger picks it up from its last recorded step: a request from an external scheduler that calls your service, or a worker you run on another host. If a worker on another host also processes these jobs, have `runJob` claim the row first, for example `UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', claimed_at = now() WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'queued' RETURNING id`, and skip the job when no row comes back, so the two never run it at once. pg-boss polls by default, so it runs over the pooled connection string (`pooled.db.prisma.io`). Graphile Worker listens with `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` by default, and so does pg-boss when you turn on `useListenNotify`; give those connections the direct connection string (`db.prisma.io`), because the pooler runs in transaction mode ([Connection pooling](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connection-pooling), [pg-boss constructor](https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss/blob/master/docs/api/constructor.md), [Graphile Worker FAQ](https://worker.graphile.org/docs/faq)). Compute doesn't require Prisma ORM or Prisma Postgres; the examples on this page use pg-boss and its own `pg` pool.

Know the limits before you rely on it:

- `waitUntil` and `KeepAwakeGuard` are best effort ([Keeping instances awake](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/keeping-instances-awake)). They keep the current instance from scaling to zero, but they don't make work durable, retry failures, or carry work through a restart or a new deployment.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [Where does Prisma Compute fit?](https://www.prisma.io#where-does-prisma-compute-fit)
payload.content:
- Compute focuses on HTTP services and has no built-in cron scheduler today ([Known limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations#runtime)); native cron is planned for early 2027. A job that has to run when no request arrives needs an external scheduler that calls your service, or a worker on another host.
- An instance kept awake is running, so it bills provisioned memory for the whole time, even while the job mostly waits ([Compute pricing](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/pricing)).
- Compute runs TypeScript on Bun and doesn't run Python, Go or Docker images ([Compute FAQ](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/faq)). A job that needs one of those belongs on a container host or in Cloud Run jobs.
- Pooled Prisma Postgres connections end any single query after 10 minutes. Long queries and `LISTEN` go over the direct connection, which allows 10 connections on Free and Starter, 50 on Pro and 100 on Business, with 5 reserved for platform operations ([Connection pooling](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connection-pooling)).

If the job must not be lost and runs for an hour or more, or must start at fixed times, keep the queue in Prisma Postgres if you like, and run the worker on Railway, Render or Fly.io, or hand the job to a durable workflow service.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)
payload.content:
## [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)

Treat any work that can take longer than a few seconds as a job from the start: the handler validates the input, saves the job and returns its id. Test with production-sized data, because a job that takes 20 seconds on a sample file can take 20 minutes on a real customer's file.

Log the job id at each stage, and alert on jobs that have been active or retrying for longer than you expect. pg-boss's `getQueue()` returns a queue's queued, active and failed counts; for your own table, a query on `status` and `updated_at` does it.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > My background job stops when my serverless function times out. Where should long-running tasks run? > [When this fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#when-this-fix-doesnt-apply)
payload.content:
## [When this fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#when-this-fix-doesnt-apply)

If the work is a response the user is waiting for, such as a streamed AI answer, a queue adds a round trip the user doesn't need. Start streaming the response early instead: on Prisma Compute, a response that has started streaming isn't cut off at 60 seconds. [AI chat responses cut off by a timeout](https://www.prisma.io/compute/ai-chat-timeout-streaming) covers that case.

If the job should run on a schedule, every night or every 5 minutes, the question is what starts it, not where it runs. See [scheduled jobs that don't run](https://www.prisma.io/compute/scheduled-jobs-not-running).

If the job fails on the first attempt every time, more time or retries won't fix it. Run it locally against a copy of the data, with the same input, and find the error first.

payload.section: API key works locally but is missing after deployment: where do production secrets go?
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > API key works locally but is missing after deployment: where do production secrets go?
payload.content:
## API key works locally but is missing after deployment: where do production secrets go?

`.env` file that Git ignores, so the deployed app never receives it. Production secrets go in your host's environment variable settings (a dashboard page or a CLI command) under the exact name your code reads, set for the environment you deployed (many hosts, such as Vercel and Netlify, hold separate values for production and previews). Then deploy again, because on Vercel, Netlify and many other hosts a changed variable applies only to new deployments. Keep the key out of variables with a public prefix such as `NEXT_PUBLIC_` or `VITE_`, which are copied into browser JavaScript at build time. On [Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute), the app reads the key through its service input, and

`npx prisma@latest project env add PAYMENTS_API_KEY --role production` stores the value for the next deploy.
[Gregory Boch](https://github.com/gregory-boch-prisma)10 min read

Your app reads the key from the environment (`process.env`, or `import.meta.env` in Vite), and on your machine something fills that in from a `.env` file: Next.js loads it into `process.env`, Vite loads it into `import.meta.env` (and exposes only `VITE_` values to browser code), and plain Node.js apps use `dotenv` or `node --env-file`. That file is in `.gitignore`, so it isn't in the repository your host deploys from. The deployed app starts with only the variables the host gives it, and the key isn't one of them until you add it in the host's settings and deploy again.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The fix below works on any host. Every host and framework behavior on this page links to its documentation, checked on October 22, 2026.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [Why the key is there locally and missing in production](https://www.prisma.io#why-the-key-is-there-locally-and-missing-in-production)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > API key works locally but is missing after deployment: where do production secrets go? > [Why the key is there locally and missing in production](https://www.prisma.io#why-the-key-is-there-locally-and-missing-in-production)
payload.content:
## [Why the key is there locally and missing in production](https://www.prisma.io#why-the-key-is-there-locally-and-missing-in-production)

A `.env` file is a convenience for development. Git doesn't commit it, so a host that builds from your repository never sees it. In production, variables come from the platform: [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/environment-variables), [Netlify](https://docs.netlify.com/build/environment-variables/overview/), [Render](https://render.com/docs/configure-environment-variables), [Railway](https://docs.railway.com/variables) and [Fly.io](https://fly.io/docs/apps/secrets/) each store them per project, service or app and pass them to your code as environment variables.

TypeScript doesn't catch the gap. With `@types/node`, `process.env.PAYMENTS_API_KEY` has the type `string | undefined` ([process.d.ts](https://github.com/DefinitelyTyped/DefinitelyTyped/blob/master/types/node/process.d.ts)), and a non-null assertion such as `process.env.PAYMENTS_API_KEY!` satisfies the compiler without supplying a value. The first sign is often a `401` from the API you call, or a client library that throws because its key is `undefined`.

payload.content:
## [Find which check fails](https://www.prisma.io#find-which-check-fails)

What you see points to the cause. Run the check before you change anything.

| What you see | Likely cause | Check | 
|---|---|---|
| `undefined` in server code on every request | The variable isn't set on the host, or is set under a different name | The host's variable list for that project or service. Names are case-sensitive. | 
| Works in a preview deployment but not in production, or the reverse | The variable is set for one environment only | The environments or deploy contexts the variable applies to | 
| Still `undefined` after you added it | The running deployment is older than the change | Whether a deployment finished after you saved the variable | 
| `undefined` in browser code | The code runs in the browser, where server-only variables don't exist | Whether the code runs in a client component or a Vite client module | 
| The build fails, or a public value is empty in the browser | The variable isn't available to the build | The variable's scope (build or runtime) and where the build runs | 
| A public value is empty only in deploys built by CI | The CI job doesn't pass the secret to the build step | The workflow's `env:` block for the build step | 
| The app exits at startup with an error about a missing `.env` file | The start script runs `node --env-file=.env` and the file isn't on the server | The `start` script in `package.json` |

| The app exits at startup with an error about a missing `.env` file | The start script runs `node --env-file=.env` and the file isn't on the server | The `start` script in `package.json` | 

The last row has a specific cause: [Node.js throws](https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html#--env-filefile) when the file passed to `--env-file` doesn't exist. Use `--env-file-if-exists=.env` (Node.js 22.9 or newer, no longer experimental since 22.21 and 24.10) in a script that also runs in production, or drop the flag there. When both the environment and the file set a variable, Node.js keeps the environment's value.

payload.content:
## [1. List every variable the code reads](https://www.prisma.io#1-list-every-variable-the-code-reads)

Search the code for environment reads and compare the list with your `.env` file:

Without a path, `git grep` searches every tracked file, so it finds reads in `app/`, `src/` or anywhere else. The pattern also matches bracket access (`process.env["PAYMENTS_API_KEY"]`) and destructuring (`const { PAYMENTS_API_KEY } = process.env`), so read each match for the names it uses.

Check the exact spelling, including case and prefix. `PAYMENTS_API_KEY` and `PAYMENT_API_KEY` are different variables, and a host integration can add a variable under a name of its own choosing.

payload.content:
## [2. Add the variables on the host, for the right environment](https://www.prisma.io#2-add-the-variables-on-the-host-for-the-right-environment)

Set each variable where the host expects it, for the environment the failing deployment belongs to. Hosts with preview or staging environments (Vercel, Netlify, [Railway](https://docs.railway.com/environments) and Prisma Compute, for example) keep separate values per environment, so a key saved only for previews is missing in production.

These hosts are ordered alphabetically:

| Host | Where to set it | When a change takes effect | 
|---|---|---|
| Fly.io | `fly secrets set PAYMENTS_API_KEY=...` | [Immediately](https://fly.io/docs/apps/secrets/): the command updates and restarts each Machine. With `--stage`, when Machines are next started or updated, for example by `fly deploy`. Runtime secrets aren't available while Fly.io builds the image, which has separate build secrets. | 
| Netlify | Project configuration, Environment variables, or `netlify env:set` | [After a new build and deploy](https://docs.netlify.com/build/environment-variables/get-started/). On Pro and Enterprise plans, a variable can be [limited to scopes](https://docs.netlify.com/build/environment-variables/overview/) (Builds, Functions, Runtime, Post processing), so a Functions-only key isn't available to the build. | 
| Prisma Compute | `npx prisma@latest project env add PAYMENTS_API_KEY=... --role production`, with the app reading the key through its service input ([details below](https://www.prisma.io#setting-production-secrets-on-prisma-compute)) | [On the next deploy](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/environment-variables). Saving a variable doesn't change existing deployments or start a deploy. |

payload.content:
| Railway | The service's Variables tab | [After you review and deploy](https://docs.railway.com/variables) the staged changes. Variables are available to the build and to the running service. | 
| Render | The service's Environment page in the dashboard | [Your choice when saving](https://render.com/docs/configure-environment-variables): rebuild and deploy, redeploy the existing build, or save only and apply on the next deploy. | 
| Vercel | Project settings, Environment Variables, or `vercel env add` | [Only on new deployments](https://vercel.com/docs/environment-variables/managing-environment-variables). Choose Production, Preview (all branches or one) or Development for each variable. | 

Other hosts and setups follow the same pattern:

- Heroku: `heroku config:set PAYMENTS_API_KEY=...`. Setting a config var [restarts the app and creates a new release](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/config-vars).
- Docker: pass variables when the container starts, with `docker run --env` or `--env-file` ([docker run reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/)). Don't set secrets with `ENV` or `ARG` in the Dockerfile: Docker's docs say [they persist in the final image](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/secrets/).
- Kubernetes: store the key in a Secret and reference it from the container's `env` with `secretKeyRef` ([Kubernetes docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/distribute-credentials-secure/)).

- Amazon ECS: reference the Secrets Manager secret in the task definition's `secrets` list and give the task execution role permission to read it. The container receives the value when it starts, so after rotating the secret, launch a new task or force a new deployment ([Amazon ECS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/secrets-envvar-secrets-manager.html)).

For secrets, [systemd's documentation](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.exec.html) recommends `LoadCredential=`, which passes them as files, because environment variables are inherited by child processes.

payload.content:
## [3. Keep the key in server code](https://www.prisma.io#3-keep-the-key-in-server-code)

A public prefix publishes the value. [Next.js](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/environment-variables) replaces `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_*` references with their values during `next build` and includes them in the JavaScript sent to the browser. [Vite](https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode) does the same for `VITE_*` variables and says they shouldn't contain API keys. If browser code needs the result of an API call, call the API from a route handler, server action or backend endpoint that reads the unprefixed variable, and return only the data the page needs.

Build-time inlining also explains a public value that stays empty or old in the browser. Next.js reads `NEXT_PUBLIC_` values from the environment where `next build` runs and doesn't pick up later changes, so the build needs them and you have to rebuild after changing one. Server-only variables are read when the code runs: in Next.js, a page that renders per request reads `process.env` at that point.

If a CI job runs the build, map each value the build needs into the build step. In GitHub Actions, a step gets a secret only through the [`secrets` context](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets), and a secret that isn't set evaluates to an empty string instead of failing the job:

payload.content:
## [Setting production secrets on Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io#setting-production-secrets-on-prisma-compute)

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute) hosts TypeScript apps built for Node.js, Bun or Next.js; deployed apps run on Bun. Prisma Compute fits when you want a missing key to stop the deploy instead of reaching production as `undefined`: in a [Prisma Composer](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer) app, the deploy fails and names any variable bound with `envSecret` that is set neither on the platform nor in the deploying shell ([Deploying](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/deploying#ci)). Compute doesn't require Prisma ORM or Prisma Postgres, so the rest of this section applies to any app you deploy there.

On Compute, the fix has two parts, because the code reads the key differently. The CLI's `deploy` command, [deploy on push](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/deploy-on-push) and the Deploy Button all deploy a [Prisma Composer](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer) app; only the REST API, whose endpoint is marked experimental, deploys without one ([Deployments](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/deployments)). In a Composer app, application code doesn't read `process.env`, so when you move an existing app over, its `process.env` reads become service input ([Compute FAQ](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/faq)).

First, declare the key as a `secretString()` field of the service's input, bind it in `module.ts` with `envSecret("PAYMENTS_API_KEY")`, and read it with `service.input()` ([Service input](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/service-input)). Your code receives a box that redacts the value in logs and JSON, and `.expose()` returns it where you pass it to the API client.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > API key works locally but is missing after deployment: where do production secrets go? > [Setting production secrets on Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io#setting-production-secrets-on-prisma-compute)
payload.content:
Then store the value that binding names, as a [project environment variable](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/environment-variables). Variables come in three layers: production, preview for every preview deploy, and overrides for a single preview branch. With only the name, the CLI reads the value from a variable of the same name in your shell, so export it first (for example from your secret manager's CLI) and the key doesn't appear in the command. With the production key exported as `PAYMENTS_API_KEY`, run:

Every preview deploy receives the preview value, so give previews a separate test or restricted key, not the production one. Export that key as `PAYMENTS_API_KEY` in the same shell, then run:

`project env` commands target the project the directory is linked to; in CI, pass `--project <id-or-name>` on each command instead ([Known limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations#cli)). `add` fails if the key already exists in that scope; use `update` to replace a value. `--branch <name>` sets an override for one preview branch, and `--file .env.production` imports a dotenv file instead of a single key. `list` shows names and metadata, never values ([project command reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/project)). Running the CLI with `npx` needs Node.js 22.18 or newer on the 22 line, 24.11 or newer on the 24 line, or 26 or newer.

A deploy can also seed the value: when a stage lacks the variable, the deploy copies it from the deploying shell ([Deploying](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/deploying)). So a deploy from your laptop can succeed while a fresh CI stage needs the value exported in the CI job.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > API key works locally but is missing after deployment: where do production secrets go? > [Setting production secrets on Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io#setting-production-secrets-on-prisma-compute)
payload.content:
Values resolve at deploy time, so deploy again after any change: run `deploy`, push to the default branch if deploy on push is set up, or promote a version, which rebuilds it with the production variables ([Compute FAQ](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/faq#how-do-i-rotate-a-secret)).

Two details matter for Next.js. `deploy` doesn't build for you: you run the build before `deploy`, locally or in CI, and deploy on push runs your build command in GitHub Actions ([Known limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations)). So `NEXT_PUBLIC_` values come from the environment where `next build` ran. And pages that read runtime configuration need `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` ([Compute FAQ](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/faq)).

Know the limits before you rely on it:

- Values are write-only. The CLI, the API and the Console never return them, and there is no command to pull them into a local `.env`, so keep the source copy in a secret manager.
- You set values with the CLI, or a deploy copies missing ones from the deploying shell. The Console lists variable names, never values.
- Keys must match `[A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]*`, and each value can be up to 8 KB. A larger credential, such as a long certificate chain, needs another delivery method, such as fetching it from a secret manager at startup.
- A changed value needs a new deployment. Prisma Compute has no documented integration that reads values from an external secret manager while the app runs.

If your app already runs on Vercel, Netlify, Render, Railway or Fly.io, moving hosts doesn't fix a missing variable. Set it where the app runs and redeploy there.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > API key works locally but is missing after deployment: where do production secrets go? > [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)
payload.content:
## [How to prevent it](https://www.prisma.io#how-to-prevent-it)

Commit a `.env.example` that lists every variable name with a placeholder value, and update it in the same change that adds a new `process.env` read. Keep the startup check from step 5, so a deploy with a missing key fails in the logs with the variable's name. Store the real values in one place you control, such as a password manager or a secret manager, and copy them to each host and CI system from there.

Never log a whole `process.env` object or a request that includes an `Authorization` header. If a key ends up in a commit or a log, rotate it with the provider before you clean up: [GitHub's guide](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/removing-sensitive-data-from-a-repository) puts revoking or rotating the secret first.

payload.content:
## [When this fix doesn't apply](https://www.prisma.io#when-this-fix-doesnt-apply)

If the variable is set and the app still gets a `401` or `403`, the key arrives but is wrong: a test key in production, a revoked key, or a key from another account. Compare the key's prefix or last characters with the provider's dashboard instead of printing it.

If the missing value is `DATABASE_URL` and you don't have a database yet, follow the [DATABASE\_URL guide](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/database-url-missing). For how to separate production and preview credentials, rotate them and hand them over to a contractor, see [where database passwords and API keys go when you deploy](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-app-secrets).

payload.content:
## Where should I host a small inventory app used by several staff members?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)fits a small TypeScript team that wants the app and database in one project. Vercel or Netlify can also host the app while Prisma Postgres stores inventory. Keep stock in the database and make a failed or repeated request part of the workflow you test.

Two staff members can both see the last item in stock. Hosting the app makes it available to them, but it does not make a read-then-write stock calculation safe. Put the acceptance rule in the database update so the server can tell one person that the item is no longer available.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The linked host and PostgreSQL documentation was checked on October 19, 2026. Prisma ORM is optional.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host a small inventory app used by several staff members? > [What does a shared inventory app need?](https://www.prisma.io#what-does-a-shared-inventory-app-need)
payload.content:
## [What does a shared inventory app need?](https://www.prisma.io#what-does-a-shared-inventory-app-need)

Use one authoritative stock record, individual staff logins and a server that checks which account or location each person may access. Record adjustments with a reason and staff identity when the business needs an audit trail. A shared platform login or a database password distributed to every browser is unnecessary.

Decide whether a click reserves stock, sells it or records a physical count. Those operations have different rules. Also decide what happens if the browser retries a request after losing the response. An app that decrements stock twice for the same sale can be wrong while every SQL statement succeeds.

## [Which app and database hosting setup fits?](https://www.prisma.io#which-app-and-database-hosting-setup-fits)

These options are ordered alphabetically by app host.

| App host | When to choose it | What remains your responsibility | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify + Prisma Postgres | Your app already uses [Netlify's framework deployment workflow](https://docs.netlify.com/deploy/deploy-overview/). | Deploy server features, configure database access and implement staff permissions. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | You want the TypeScript app and its database declared in one project. | Configure the module, authentication, migrations and inventory rules. | 
| Vercel + Prisma Postgres | Your Next.js app already uses [Vercel deployments](https://vercel.com/docs/deployments). | Configure the server's database URL and test the actual inventory endpoints. | 

For a new project, Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres let the team keep deployment and database setup together. Follow the [Composer database guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases) for a declared dependency, or keep an existing PostgreSQL client and configure a separately managed database URL. Place the database-calling server [near the database](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/nodejs-database-regions).

payload.content:
## [2. Test an atomic stock change](https://www.prisma.io#2-test-an-atomic-stock-change)

In a fresh development database, run this example through its [direct connection](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database). Use migrations for the real schema.

The update returns `LAST-ITEM` with quantity `0`. A second staff request running the same update returns no rows. Under PostgreSQL's default Read Committed isolation, an update waiting for a concurrent writer rechecks its condition against the updated row. See the [transaction isolation documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html).

In application code, derive the business account from the verified staff session. Bind the SKU and requested quantity as parameters, validate that the quantity is a positive integer, and handle a zero-row result explicitly. Do not read a number into the browser and later save a replacement number calculated from that stale value.

## [3. Make a sale more than a stock decrement](https://www.prisma.io#3-make-a-sale-more-than-a-stock-decrement)

If a sale also creates an order, adjustment record or reservation, group the required database changes in one [transaction](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/customer-order-transactions). Add a unique business request identifier so retries can return an existing result instead of decrementing stock twice. The single-statement example above demonstrates the stock boundary, not a complete retry-safe checkout.

Test concurrency using two sessions attempting the last item. Also test a double click, a lost response, a return and a staff account from another business. The UI should preserve the user's intent when a request fails and refresh the stock value after a successful operation.

## [4. Verify the deployed workflow with the business owner](https://www.prisma.io#4-verify-the-deployed-workflow-with-the-business-owner)

Use a separate review environment with fictional products. Confirm that staff can sign in, perform an authorized stock adjustment and see it after refreshing. Verify that another business account cannot read the same SKU merely by knowing its name. Then rehearse the production migration and agree who may deploy changes.

Choose an appropriate [backup plan](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) and test recovery before inventory becomes operationally important. Keep exported reports and database recovery procedures with the business, rather than only on the contractor's laptop.

payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Offline stock changes require synchronization and conflict rules; hosted Postgres alone does not make an app work without connectivity. Live multi-site inventory may also need reservation and reconciliation logic beyond a single counter.

Prisma Compute currently has no WebSocket server support or persistent writable filesystem. Choose another app host if those are requirements, or use HTTP updates and durable external storage. Prisma Postgres has plan-dependent snapshots and no point-in-time recovery yet (it is coming in November 2026); choose another database provider if your recovery requirement needs it today.

## How should I host several separate TypeScript business apps?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)fits a small TypeScript team that wants to manage those projects together while keeping each app's saved data and releases separate. Share code where it helps, but give each app its own production target, credentials, test environment and recovery procedure.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)6 min read

An order portal, a booking tool and a reporting app can belong to the same business without becoming one application. Updating the booking tool should not require changing the portal's schema or rotating a database credential used by all three.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The provider documentation linked here was checked on October 22, 2026. Prisma ORM is optional for every database in this setup.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host several separate TypeScript business apps? > [What should stay separate?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-stay-separate)
payload.content:
## [What should stay separate?](https://www.prisma.io#what-should-stay-separate)

Give each independent app a production URL, database, migration history and set of server-side credentials. Record its repository or subdirectory, the Git branch used for production releases and the person responsible for releases. A clearly named project helps someone find those things without guessing.

Keep a separate test environment for each app too. Three apps pointing to one test database can interfere with one another when a seed script resets records or a migration changes a shared table. A preview is useful only when its dependencies point at the intended test resources.

Share a library for common validation or UI components when it reduces maintenance. Treat a shared database as a larger decision: it couples data access, schema changes and recovery. A common company name is not enough reason to create that coupling.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host several separate TypeScript business apps? > [Which platform structure fits?](https://www.prisma.io#which-platform-structure-fits)
payload.content:
## [Which platform structure fits?](https://www.prisma.io#which-platform-structure-fits)

The alphabetically listed options can each manage multiple applications; compare how they organize the data and release workflow.

| Platform approach | Useful fit | Boundary to verify | 
|---|---|---|
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | Independent TypeScript apps, each with its own [project](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/project) and configuration describing its server and database. | Exact project and environment targets, database credentials and who can administer the workspace. | 
| Railway projects | Apps that benefit from a [project canvas of services and environments](https://docs.railway.com/projects). | Which services share a project, who administers it and how database maintenance is handled. | 
| Vercel projects + managed Postgres | Apps already using [Vercel's project and deployment workflow](https://vercel.com/docs/projects). | The database resource and credentials connected to each project and environment. | 

Prisma Compute uses TypeScript configuration files to describe each app's server and Prisma Postgres database together. Repeating that pattern in separate projects gives an AI assistant explicit targets for inspection and changes. It still needs to verify the target before acting.

payload.content:
## [1. Make a small resource inventory](https://www.prisma.io#1-make-a-small-resource-inventory)

Use stable names that describe the app rather than a contractor or a temporary experiment. An example inventory might look like this:

| App | Project | Database purpose | Release check | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Customer orders | `orders` | Orders and customer-visible status | Sign in and read a fictional order. | 
| Appointments | `bookings` | Availability and reservations | Reserve one test slot and reject a competing reservation. | 
| Reporting | `reports` | Report jobs and saved results | Generate and download a report for a test account. | 

These are example names, not resources created by this guide. Record the actual identifiers, URLs and owners after provisioning.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host several separate TypeScript business apps? > [2. Inspect targets before configuring a deployment](https://www.prisma.io#2-inspect-targets-before-configuring-a-deployment)
payload.content:
## [2. Inspect targets before configuring a deployment](https://www.prisma.io#2-inspect-targets-before-configuring-a-deployment)

A workspace is the administrative group containing your projects. Sign in, then use [workspace sessions](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/auth) to select the intended workspace before using the [project CLI](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/project). If the list shows several, run `npx prisma@latest auth workspace use YOUR_WORKSPACE_ID`, replacing `YOUR_WORKSPACE_ID` with the intended identifier from that list:

Replace `orders` with an existing project's actual name or identifier. The output depends on your account. A folder name does not select the cloud project. `npx prisma@latest project show` without a name shows its local project link; the deploy target comes from the exported app name in `module.ts` or the explicit `--name` flag below. Check that name as well as the inspected project before deploying.

For each app, complete [Composer getting started](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/getting-started) to create `module.ts`, `service.ts`, the build script and deploy configuration. Composer is the framework that reads these TypeScript files and creates the server and its resources. Follow [Databases](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases) to connect the app to its own database, with one app responsible for its migrations.

The first [deploy](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/deploy) creates the project and the resources described by `module.ts`. Choose an unused project name for a new app and configure a supported region before that first deploy. An existing app should reuse its verified project rather than create another copy.

payload.section: [3. Give each app its own credentials and test data](https://www.prisma.io#3-give-each-app-its-own-credentials-and-test-data)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host several separate TypeScript business apps? > [3. Give each app its own credentials and test data](https://www.prisma.io#3-give-each-app-its-own-credentials-and-test-data)
payload.content:
## [3. Give each app its own credentials and test data](https://www.prisma.io#3-give-each-app-its-own-credentials-and-test-data)

Give each app its own Prisma Postgres database and connect it only to the one it owns. For other configuration and credentials, [Service input](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/service-input) shows the fields to add to `service.ts`, their bindings in `module.ts` and the server-side read. Supply separate [environment values](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/environment-variables) for production and test deployments. A test deployment must not receive another app's production URL. `deploy --name` selects the deployment project but does not change the directory's local project link. For every `project env` command, pass the intended app's explicit `--project` value as well as its production, preview or branch scope. For example, once `orders` exists, `npx prisma@latest project env list --project orders --role preview` inspects that project's preview variable names without displaying their values. This avoids writing credentials to a different project linked by a parent directory.

Review who can administer the projects and which projects an automation credential can affect. Separate projects may still be accessible to the same administrators and automation credentials. If the apps belong to different clients, choose the workspace and account ownership around that access requirement.

payload.content:
## [4. Release and recover one app at a time](https://www.prisma.io#4-release-and-recover-one-app-at-a-time)

From one configured app's directory, build and deploy its test environment. This example selects the supported `us-east-1` region; choose an appropriate [region](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/deploy) before the first deploy. For example, use `orders` only after checking that it is the intended project name:

The deploy prints the service URL and created resource identifiers; these vary by account. `review` names an [isolated deployment stage](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/deploying#production-and-stages). The module's own database is created for that stage; manually supplied URLs must point to separate test resources. Repeat from the other apps' directories with their own names and configurations. Apply each app's migrations to its review database before acceptance tests. With `rawPostgres()` or a manually supplied URL, use that database's direct connection; a configured `postgres()` data contract can apply migrations during deployment. Production deployment omits `--stage review`.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [4. Release and recover one app at a time](https://www.prisma.io#4-release-and-recover-one-app-at-a-time)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > How should I host several separate TypeScript business apps? > [4. Release and recover one app at a time](https://www.prisma.io#4-release-and-recover-one-app-at-a-time)
payload.content:
For [deploy on push](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/deploy-on-push), connect each project to GitHub and configure a deployment job for each app. The guide's example runs from the repository root by default; copying it once does not deploy all apps in a shared repository. Set the deploy action's `working-directory`, `build-command` and `module` inputs for that app. If the lockfile is at the workspace root, also set `install-command` to install dependencies from that root; the action's automatic detection only checks its working directory. Set each module's exported app name to its intended project, such as `orders`, before enabling the action. The action does not carry over the earlier CLI `--name` override; its module name must select the same verified project. The connection permits authentication; the workflow installs dependencies, builds and deploys. Check each job's project target before relying on push deployment.

After approval, release the intended app with its production credentials, configuration and migration plan. For a first production database managed through `rawPostgres()` or a supplied URL, provision it with customer traffic disabled, apply migrations through its direct connection, then verify before enabling customers. Verify its public URL and representative workflow. A shared dependency update may justify testing all three apps, but it should not silently change all three databases.

payload.section: [4. Release and recover one app at a time](https://www.prisma.io#4-release-and-recover-one-app-at-a-time)

payload.content: Choose and rehearse a [backup and restore procedure](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) for each database. Restoring one app should not rewind records another app needs. Review usage by app and the scope of [spending controls](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-hosting-spending-controls); resource separation does not automatically create independent billing limits.

payload.content:
## [When should I use a different boundary?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-use-a-different-boundary)

Use stronger account separation when separate clients, legal owners or teams must control their own administration and billing. Conversely, components that always release together and share one domain model may belong in one application with several services rather than several independent projects.

Check [Compute's runtime limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations) for each app separately. An app requiring a persistent local disk or a WebSocket server may need a different host while the other TypeScript apps stay on Compute. Prisma Postgres remains usable from those hosts with an ordinary PostgreSQL client.

## Where can I host a Next.js API for form submissions?

[Prisma Compute](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute)with

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)fits a small TypeScript app that needs its server and saved submissions in one project. Vercel and Netlify also run Next.js server features. Choose a hosted form service when collecting standard enquiries is the whole requirement; choose an application server when submissions drive your own business workflow.

[Søren Bramer Schmidt](https://github.com/sorenbs)6 min read

A contact page loading successfully does not prove its form works. The submission needs a server that receives the request, rejects invalid input and records a result before telling the browser it succeeded. Test that path at the deployed URL.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The linked provider and Next.js documentation was checked on October 23, 2026. Prisma ORM is optional.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.section: [What kind of hosting does my form need?](https://www.prisma.io#what-kind-of-hosting-does-my-form-need)
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a Next.js API for form submissions? > [What kind of hosting does my form need?](https://www.prisma.io#what-kind-of-hosting-does-my-form-need)
payload.content:
## [What kind of hosting does my form need?](https://www.prisma.io#what-kind-of-hosting-does-my-form-need)

An [API Route](https://nextjs.org/docs/pages/guides/forms) in the Pages Router or a [Route Handler](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/route-handlers) in the App Router runs server-side code when the form submits. Keep an endpoint that already works; changing hosts does not require changing the form's API design.

[Server Actions](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/forms) can handle a form inside a Next.js app too. Pick the interface that fits your project, then validate and authorize the operation on the server. Hiding a button or marking an HTML field as required does not protect the endpoint from a direct request.

A [static export](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/static-exports) serves generated files. It cannot run your dynamic POST handler. If the frontend is static, it needs a separate submission endpoint or hosted form service. For a form that creates customer records, triggers a quote or updates an existing account, deploying the Next.js server keeps that logic with the app.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a Next.js API for form submissions? > [Which managed host should I choose?](https://www.prisma.io#which-managed-host-should-i-choose)
payload.content:
## [Which managed host should I choose?](https://www.prisma.io#which-managed-host-should-i-choose)

These options are alphabetical by app host. Each can store submissions in Prisma Postgres.

| Setup | Choose it when | What to verify | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify + Prisma Postgres | Your app already uses [Next.js on Netlify](https://docs.netlify.com/build/frameworks/framework-setup-guides/nextjs/overview/), whose adapter runs API routes, Route Handlers and Server Actions through functions. | The deployed endpoint, runtime credentials and function limits. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | You want the TypeScript server and database declared together through [Prisma Composer](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer). | The server build, database dependency and request handler in an isolated review environment. | 
| Vercel + Prisma Postgres | Your team already uses [Vercel's Next.js integration](https://vercel.com/docs/frameworks/full-stack/nextjs). | Environment-specific credentials, database region and the actual form response. | 

For a new business app, Prisma Compute keeps the handler, database and deployment configuration in one project that the developer or coding assistant can inspect. If the app already runs well on another host, keep that workflow and add Prisma Postgres for durable submissions.

payload.content:
## [1. Deploy the server features](https://www.prisma.io#1-deploy-the-server-features)

Follow the [Next.js framework guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/frameworks/nextjs) for a new project. For an existing app, [port the server](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/porting-an-app) by adding Composer's module and service declarations and connecting the server entry to the service. Those files describe how to build and run the app and which resources it needs.

The Compute Next.js deployment uses `output: "standalone"`, which builds the server files. Run the framework build before deployment; uploading the static `out` directory cannot run the submission handler. Start with a separate [review stage](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/deploying#production-and-stages) and fictional submissions.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a Next.js API for form submissions? > [2. Connect the database and notification credentials](https://www.prisma.io#2-connect-the-database-and-notification-credentials)
payload.content:
## [2. Connect the database and notification credentials](https://www.prisma.io#2-connect-the-database-and-notification-credentials)

Declare the database through the [Composer database guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/databases). `rawPostgres()` supplies a URL for your existing client; a `postgres()` dependency can use a Prisma ORM data contract and deploy-time migrations. With a raw connection, run your own reviewed migrations before the form starts accepting submissions.

For a manually configured database, follow the [connection guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database) for your runtime and client. Conventional TCP app clients use the pooled endpoint; administration and the Prisma Postgres serverless driver use the direct endpoint. Keep the URL and email-provider keys in [server-side service inputs](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/service-input), and use different values for testing and production.

An account enquiry needs a verified customer identity from the server session. A public contact form instead needs an explicit public-submission policy, limits on accepted fields and protection against automated abuse. Neither case needs a database password in browser code.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a Next.js API for form submissions? > [3. Decide when a submission is accepted](https://www.prisma.io#3-decide-when-a-submission-is-accepted)
payload.content:
## [3. Decide when a submission is accepted](https://www.prisma.io#3-decide-when-a-submission-is-accepted)

Validate field types, length and business rules before saving. Cap request bodies and reject unsupported content types before expensive parsing. For a cookie-authenticated mutation, apply the framework's appropriate cross-site request protection as well as authentication and authorization. For public forms, add request-rate limits and an abuse challenge where needed; a hidden field alone is not a complete defence.

Save the accepted submission before returning a success response. Give it an identifier the user and staff can refer to. If the browser retries after losing the response, a stable request key can let the server return the existing result. Scope that key to the correct actor or workflow and reject reuse with different input.

If accepting a submission also creates related records, use a [database transaction](https://www.prisma.io/postgres/customer-order-transactions). Keep notification work retryable. For example, commit an enquiry and a pending-email record together, then let a deployed worker deliver that email and record its outcome. That design requires a worker and retry policy; writing a pending row by itself does not send anything.

payload.title: Prisma ORM
payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where can I host a Next.js API for form submissions? > [4. Test through the public review URL](https://www.prisma.io#4-test-through-the-public-review-url)
payload.content:
## [4. Test through the public review URL](https://www.prisma.io#4-test-through-the-public-review-url)

Submit a fictional enquiry, check its saved record and reload the app to verify it persists. Submit malformed data and confirm the server rejects it. Then retry a previously accepted request and check that staff do not get duplicate records.

Also test another account's identifiers for a private form, a failed database write and a failed notification. The page should show a useful error or an accepted-with-notification-pending result according to the policy you implemented. Use request and submission identifiers in access-controlled logs, keeping secret keys and full customer messages out of them.

Release the approved commit with production credentials and reviewed migrations, then repeat a controlled acceptance check at the production URL. Confirm the database target before enabling the form for customers. Choose a [backup policy](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups) for submissions the business depends on.

payload.content:
## [When should I choose a different setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-a-different-setup)

A standard enquiry form may be easier to operate with a hosted form product if you do not need custom account rules, transactions or staff workflows. Keeping a static frontend with such a service can be a reasonable choice.

Prisma Compute runs deployed services on Bun. Check [runtime compatibility and request limits](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations), including the 60-second deadline to start responding and the absence of a persistent filesystem. Use external object storage for attachments and a durable worker for lengthy processing. A success response must reflect accepted work that can be recovered after the server process stops.

## Where should I host a Next.js app with Stripe subscriptions?

[Prisma Postgres](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres)fits a small TypeScript team that wants the application and database in one project. Vercel or Netlify with Prisma Postgres also work well when you already use their Next.js deployment workflow. Choose the host around the app; design webhook verification, retries and access decisions explicitly.

A subscription app has work to do after the checkout tab closes. A renewal can fail, a customer can cancel, and an event can arrive again after your handler has already processed it. Your deployment needs to support that lifecycle, not only the payment button.

We make Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres. The linked provider and Stripe documentation was checked on October 22, 2026. Prisma ORM is optional.

payload.content:
## [What must the hosting setup support?](https://www.prisma.io#what-must-the-hosting-setup-support)

Run checkout creation, webhook verification and checks of paid feature access on the server. [Stripe Checkout](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/checkout) can collect the payment details; Postgres stores the identifiers and application state you need to recognize the customer and decide what they may use.

Give Stripe a stable, publicly reachable HTTPS webhook URL. The handler needs the unmodified request body for [signature verification](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks), so check the deployed framework route rather than assuming a handler that worked locally will receive the same bytes. A webhook route authenticates Stripe through its signature; a customer login redirect must not intercept it.

Keep app accounts, Stripe customers, subscriptions and records of processed events distinct. A unique event identifier helps recognize a repeated delivery. It does not prove that a customer owns an account or that an arbitrary subscription state should grant access.

## [Which host should I choose?](https://www.prisma.io#which-host-should-i-choose)

These options are alphabetical by app host. Each can use Prisma Postgres.

| Setup | Choose it when | Check before launch | 
|---|---|---|
| Netlify + Prisma Postgres | Your app already uses [Next.js on Netlify](https://docs.netlify.com/build/frameworks/framework-setup-guides/nextjs/overview/). | Verify the webhook route, runtime secrets and database connection in the deployed functions. | 
| Prisma Compute + Prisma Postgres | You want the TypeScript server and database configured and deployed as one application with [Prisma Composer](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer). | Build the server files, configure server-side secrets and test the full billing lifecycle. | 
| Vercel + Prisma Postgres | Your team already relies on [Vercel's Next.js integration](https://vercel.com/docs/frameworks/full-stack/nextjs). | Scope test and production credentials, and check that deployment protection permits the intended webhook endpoint. | 

For a new TypeScript business app, Prisma Compute keeps the server, database and deployment configuration together. An existing Vercel or Netlify app can keep its working host while moving its customer records to Prisma Postgres.

## [1. Build an isolated test deployment](https://www.prisma.io#1-build-an-isolated-test-deployment)

For a new app, complete the [Next.js setup guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/guides/frameworks/nextjs). For an existing app, follow [Port an existing app](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/porting-an-app) to add `module.ts` and `service.ts` before using the deploy commands below. These TypeScript configuration files tell Composer which server and database to create. Composer is the deployment framework included in the Prisma CLI. Keep `output: "standalone"` in `next.config.ts` so Next.js builds the server files Compute runs.

Before the first deployment, follow [Service input](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/service-input) to declare the billing configuration in `service.ts`, bind its values in `module.ts` and read them on the server through `service.input()`. Give the input schema a billing-disabled mode that permits missing Stripe secrets. In that mode, the app must avoid initializing Stripe and reject checkout and webhook processing. Disabling a checkout button alone does not change configuration validation. Start a new environment in this mode so it can receive its URL before a webhook signing secret exists.

With that configuration in place, choose a [supported region](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/deploy) near the database and users. The following shell example selects `us-east-1`; substitute the region you chose before the first deploy. Then sign in, build and deploy a separate test environment:

payload.content:
The deploy prints the created service URL and database identifiers; their values depend on your account. `review` is the name of this [isolated deployment stage](https://www.prisma.io/docs/composer/deploying#production-and-stages). Databases created by that module belong to the stage. Check those identifiers before testing.

Register a Stripe test webhook endpoint at your handler's path on the review URL. Bind the test API key and that endpoint's signing secret with `envSecret(...)`, then switch to billing-enabled configuration that requires both secrets. The API key authorizes calls to Stripe; the signing secret verifies incoming webhooks. The Service input guide explains how a missing stage variable is seeded from the deploying shell. Give test and production their own values, and update existing platform variables through the environment-variable workflow rather than expecting a changed shell value to replace them. A named stage does not change a manually supplied database URL or payment credential. With the test secrets supplied, rerun `npm run build` and `npx prisma@latest deploy --stage review` from the app directory before billing tests.

payload.breadcrumb: Prisma ORM > Where should I host a Next.js app with Stripe subscriptions? > [2. Apply the schema and define event processing](https://www.prisma.io#2-apply-the-schema-and-define-event-processing)
payload.content:
## [2. Apply the schema and define event processing](https://www.prisma.io#2-apply-the-schema-and-define-event-processing)

Create the customer-to-Stripe mapping, subscription state and an event-processing record through migrations. Run migrations and schema administration with the [direct database URL](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/connecting-to-your-database), while application queries use the pooled URL. The direct URL also supports administrative tools that need the same connection across several statements, such as a session using temporary tables. Keep database credentials off the browser.

For short handlers, commit the processed-event record and the related state change in one transaction before returning success. If the handler fails, a record marked complete must not remain while the corresponding change is missing. For longer work, save the verified event in a database table before returning success to Stripe. A background worker must process those saved events, retry failures and mark completed work. This hosting guide assumes the short transaction approach; a queued design also needs a deployed, monitored worker before launch.

[Stripe subscription events](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/webhooks) cover changes beyond initial payment. Handle repeated deliveries without repeating a business action, and handle out-of-order events without overwriting newer state with an older snapshot. When deliveries disagree, check the subscription's current status in Stripe. Process updates for each subscription one at a time so concurrent handlers cannot overwrite each other. Keep outbound email or other side effects retryable too.

payload.content:
## [3. Exercise the billing lifecycle with fictional customers](https://www.prisma.io#3-exercise-the-billing-lifecycle-with-fictional-customers)

In Stripe's test environment, complete a checkout, then verify the database record and the resulting access decision. Repeat an event, change its delivery order, simulate a processing failure and confirm that retrying completes the missing work once. Test renewal, payment failure and cancellation according to your chosen access policy.

Inspect delivery results in Stripe and application logs at the same time. Log the Stripe event identifier, processing status and the app's request identifier so you can match a delivery to its handler. Keep secret keys and full customer payloads out of logs. A successful HTTP response should mean the event was processed or durably accepted for processing.

payload.content:
## [4. Release production deliberately](https://www.prisma.io#4-release-production-deliberately)

After your billing tests pass in the review deployment, release the approved commit with production credentials and configuration. For an existing production database, apply its reviewed migrations before the app release. For a new database using `rawPostgres()` or a manually supplied URL, provision it with live checkout disabled, obtain its direct connection and apply migrations before accepting customer traffic. A configured `postgres()` data contract can apply migrations during deployment. Build before deploying; omitting `--stage review` targets production. Register the production webhook URL in Stripe and configure its own signing secret. If production needs its first URL, use the billing-disabled bootstrap mode described in step 1: its schema must permit absent Stripe secrets and its code must avoid initializing billing. After registering the endpoint, save the production secrets, switch to the billing-enabled configuration, rebuild and redeploy before accepting payments. Verify the URL, signature rejection and the database target before enabling live checkout.

Choose a [backup plan](https://www.prisma.io/docs/postgres/database/backups), rehearse restoration and define how to reconcile restored subscription records with Stripe. A database snapshot can predate a payment or cancellation. Review [hosting spending controls](https://www.prisma.io/compute/typescript-hosting-spending-controls) separately from the subscription prices you charge customers.

payload.content:
## [When should I choose another setup?](https://www.prisma.io#when-should-i-choose-another-setup)

Prisma Compute runs deployed services on Bun. Check the [runtime limitations](https://www.prisma.io/docs/compute/limitations) if the app depends on a native library, a persistent filesystem or a WebSocket server. Requests have 60 seconds to start responding; billing handlers should acknowledge durable acceptance promptly rather than using that limit as their processing target.

Prisma Postgres has plan-dependent daily snapshots and no point-in-time recovery yet (it is coming in November 2026). If your recovery requirement depends on restoring to a particular moment, choose a database that meets it. Managed hosting also leaves the subscription rules and webhook implementation with your team; a ready-made membership product may be less maintenance when you do not need a custom application.
